1: ---
2: stage: none
3: group: unassigned
4: info: For assistance with this Style Guide page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments-to-other-projects-and-subjects>.
5: description: Writing styles, markup, formatting, and other standards for the GitLab RESTful APIs.
6: title: Documenting REST API resources
7: ---
8: 
9: REST API resources are documented in Markdown under
10: [`/doc/api`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api). Each
11: resource has its own Markdown file, which is linked from
12: [`api_resources.md`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/doc/api/api_resources.md).
13: 
14: When modifying the Markdown or API code, also update the corresponding
15: [OpenAPI definition](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api/openapi), by running
16: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:generate` and `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:generate`.
17: To check if the OpenAPI definition needs to be updated, you can run `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:check_docs` and
18: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:check_docs`.
19: This is also checked by the `openapi-doc-check` CI/CD job that runs for commits that modify API code or documentation.
20: 
21: The Markdown topic for an API resource must include:
22: 
23: - A block that includes the HTTP method (like GET, PUT, DELETE) followed by the request path. Always start the path with a `/`. For example:
24: 
25:   ```plaintext
26:   GET /api/v4/projects/:id/repository/branches
27:   ```
28: 
29: - A detailed [description of the attributes](#request-attributes).
30: - A detailed [description of the response body](#response-attributes).
31: - A cURL example.
32: - A response body example (in JSON format).
33: 
34: After a new API documentation page is added, [add an entry in the global navigation](site_architecture/global_nav.md#add-a-navigation-entry).
35: 
36: ## Page metadata
37: 
38: When you create a new page, include a `description` metadata field
39: in the front matter that follows these guidelines for consistency:
40: 
41: - Start with "REST API to"
42: - Use action verbs that describe what users can do with the API
43: - Avoid words ending in -ing
44: - Keep to one sentence, ideally under 100 characters
45: - End with a period
46: 
47: For example:
48: 
49: ```yaml
50: ---
51: stage: Example Stage
52: group: Example Group
53: info: To determine the technical writer assigned to the Stage/Group associated with this page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments>
54: description: REST API to create, update, and delete issues.
55: title: Example page title
56: ---
57: ```
58: 
59: Additional examples:
60: 
61: - `description: REST API to retrieve CI/CD job details, retry and cancel jobs, run manual jobs, and access job logs.`
62: - `description: REST API to create, manage, and monitor CI/CD pipelines.`
63: 
64: ## API topic template
65: 
66: Use the following template to help you get started. Be sure to list any
67: required attributes first in the table.
68: 
69: ````markdown
70: ## API name
71: 
72: {{</* history */>}}
73: 
74: - History note.
75: 
76: {{</* /history */>}}
77: 
78: Use this API to ...
79: 
80: ### Operation title
81: 
82: {{</* history */>}}
83: 
84: - History note.
85: 
86: {{</* /history */>}}
87: 
88: Description of the operation.
89: 
90: ```plaintext
91: METHOD /api/v4/endpoint
92: ```
93: 
94: Supported attributes:
95: 
96: | Attribute                | Type     | Required | Description           |
97: |--------------------------|----------|----------|-----------------------|
98: | `attribute`              | datatype | Yes      | Detailed description. |
99: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
100: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
101: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
102: 
103: If successful, returns [`<status_code>`](rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes) and the following
104: response attributes:
105: 
106: | Attribute                | Type     | Description           |
107: |--------------------------|----------|-----------------------|
108: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
109: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
110: 
111: Example request:
112: 
113: ```shell
114: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
115:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/endpoint?parameters"
116: ```
117: 
118: Example response:
119: 
120: ```json
121: [
122:   {
123:   }
124: ]
125: ```
126: ````
127: 
128: ## History
129: 
130: Add [history](styleguide/availability_details.md#history)
131: to describe new or updated API calls.
132: 
133: To add history for an individual attribute, include it in the history
134: for the section. For example:
135: 
136: ```markdown
137: ### Edit a widget
138: 
139: {{</* history */>}}
140: 
141:  - `widget_message` [introduced](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.3.
142: 
143: {{</* /history */>}}
144: ```
145: 
146: If the API or attribute is deployed behind a feature flag,
147: [include the feature flag information](feature_flags.md) in the history.
148: 
149: ## Deprecations
150: 
151: To document the deprecation of an API endpoint, follow the steps to
152: [deprecate a page or topic](styleguide/deprecations_and_removals.md).
153: 
154: To deprecate an attribute:
155: 
156: 1. Add a history note.
157: 
158:    ```markdown
159:    {{</* history */>}}
160: 
161:    - `widget_name` [deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7.
162: 
163:    {{</* /history */>}}
164:    ```
165: 
166: 1. Add inline deprecation text to the description.
167: 
168:    ```markdown
169:    | Attribute     | Type   | Required | Description |
170:    |---------------|--------|----------|-------------|
171:    | `widget_name` | string | No       | [Deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7. Use `widget_id` instead. The name of the widget. |
172:    ```
173: 
174: To widely announce a deprecation, [update the REST API deprecations page](../../api/rest/deprecations.md).
175: 
176: ## API introduction
177: 
178: Each API is made of one or more operations. At the start of the topic, include information that
179: applies to all operations in the API, and a short description of the related features.
180: 
181: For consistency, try to start the introduction with: `Use this API to {verb} + [{feature}](link/to/UI/docs).`
182: This allows us to direct users to related documentation that might include more context.
183: 
184: For example:
185: 
186: - `Use this API to manage [Git branches](path/to/file).`
187: - `Use this API to interact with the [Maven package manager client](path/to/file).`
188: - `Use this API to interact with namespaces, a special resource category used to organize users and groups. For more information, see [namespaces](path/to/file).`
189: 
190: ## Operation titles
191: 
192: Start an operation title with a verb. For consistency,
193: use these verbs based on the HTTP method:
194: 
195: | HTTP method      | Verb     | Alternatives | Examples |
196: | ---------------- | -------- | ------------ | -------- |
197: | `GET` (multiple) | List all |              | `List all group access tokens` |
198: | `GET` (single)   | Retrieve | Download     | `Retrieve a group audit event`, `Download a dependency list export` |
199: | `POST`           | Create   | Add          | `Create a repository branch`, `Add a new emoji reaction` |
200: | `PUT`            | Update   | Replace      | `Update a project topic` |
201: | `PATCH`          | Update   | Modify       | `Update a freeze period`, `Modify an existing commit thread note` |
202: | `DELETE`         | Delete   |              | `Delete a feature` |
203: 
204: When possible, use the recommended verb. Alternatives might be needed in specific contexts, but
205: minimize their use to maintain consistency.
206: 
207: ## Operation descriptions
208: 
209: Each operation should include a short description that explains its use, and highlights any
210: important information. If possible, write the first sentence to broadly repeat the title of
211: the operation. For example:
212: 
213: - `List all project access tokens` -> `Lists all project access tokens.`
214: - `Delete an SSH key` -> `Deletes an SSH key from your user account.`
215: - `Retrieve an enterprise user` -> `Retrieves details on a specified enterprise user.`
216: 
217: ## Request attributes
218: 
219: You must document the request attributes in an operation. When creating the table and attribute descriptions:
220: 
221: - Use the following column names for attribute tables.
222: - List any path attributes first, then any required attributes, then sort alphabetically.
223: - Place the attribute name in code blocks using backticks (`` ` ``).
224: - Document any tier or offering information specific to an attribute in the description.
225:   - If an attribute is available for Premium, mention that it's also available for Ultimate.
226:   - Combine this tier and offering information when possible. For example: `GitLab Self-Managed, Premium and Ultimate only.`
227: 
228: ```markdown
229: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
230: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
231: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
232: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
233: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
234: ```
235: 
236: Rendered example:
237: 
238: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
239: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
240: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
241: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
242: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
243: 
244: For information about writing attribute descriptions, see the [GraphQL API description style guide](../api_graphql_styleguide.md#description-style-guide).
245: 
246: ### Conditionally required attributes
247: 
248: If an attribute is related to another item, indicate this in the attribute description.
249: 
250: Generally, this happens if one of two attributes is required or if an attribute must be enabled and configured separately.
251: 
252: First define the attribute itself, then mention any requirements. Use this format:
253: 
254:   ```markdown
255:   Required if `attribute1` is `true`.
256:   ```
257: 
258: For example:
259: 
260: | Attribute                  | Type    | Required    | Description |
261: | -------------------------- | ------- | ----------- | ----------- |
262: | `include_saml_users`       | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns users with a SAML identity. Required if `include_service_accounts` is `false`. |
263: | `include_service_accounts` | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns service account users. Required if `include_saml_users` is `false`. |
264: | `a_related_setting`        | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, does something else. Required if `include_saml_users` is `true`. |
265: 
266: ## Response attributes
267: 
268: You might sometimes need to document the response attributes in an operation. This is not usually required.
269: When creating the table and attribute descriptions:
270: 
271: - Use the following column names for attribute tables.
272: - Sort the table alphabetically.
273: - Place the attribute name in code blocks using backticks (`` ` ``).
274: - If describing an object or array, use dot notation to represent the sub-attributes. For example, `project.name` or `projects[].name`.
275: - Document any tier or offering information specific to an attribute in the description.
276:   - If an attribute is available for Premium, mention that it's also available for Ultimate.
277:   - Combine this tier and offering information when possible. For example: `GitLab Self-Managed, Premium and Ultimate only.`
278: 
279: Start the description with the following sentence, replacing `status code` with the
280: relevant [HTTP status code](../../api/rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes), for example:
281: 
282: ```markdown
283: If successful, returns [`200 OK`](../../api/rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes) and the
284: following response attributes:
285: ```
286: 
287: ```markdown
288: | Attribute      | Type          | Description |
289: | -------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
290: | `assignee_ids` | integer array | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Premium and Ultimate only. |
291: | `commits`      | object array  | Commits in the merge request diff. |
292: | `commits[].id` | string        | ID of the commit. |
293: ```
294: 
295: Rendered example:
296: 
297: | Attribute      | Type          | Description |
298: | -------------- | ------------- | ----------- |
299: | `assignee_ids` | integer array | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Premium and Ultimate only. |
300: | `commits`      | object array  | Commits in the merge request diff. |
301: | `commits[].id` | string        | ID of the commit. |
302: 
303: For information about writing attribute descriptions, see the [GraphQL API description style guide](../api_graphql_styleguide.md#description-style-guide).
304: 
305: ## cURL commands
306: 
307: - Use `https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/` as an endpoint.
308: - Wherever needed use this personal access token: `<your_access_token>`.
309: - Always put the request first. `GET` is the default so you don't have to
310:   include it.
311: - Use long option names (`--header` instead of `-H`) for legibility. (Tested in
312:   [`scripts/lint-doc.sh`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/scripts/lint-doc.sh).)
313: - Declare URLs with the `--url` parameter, and wrap the URL in double quotes (`"`).
314: - Prefer to use examples using the personal access token and don't pass data of
315:   username and password.
316: - For legibility, use the ` \ ` character and indentation to break long single-line
317:   commands apart into multiple lines.
318: 
319: | Methods                                         | Description                                            |
320: |-------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
321: | `--header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>"` | Use this method as is, whenever authentication needed. |
322: | `--request POST`                                | Use this method when creating new objects.             |
323: | `--request PUT`                                 | Use this method when updating existing objects.        |
324: | `--request DELETE`                              | Use this method when removing existing objects.        |
325: 
326: ## cURL Examples
327: 
328: The following sections include a set of [cURL](https://curl.se/) examples
329: you can use in the API documentation.
330: 
331: > [!warning]
332: > Do not use information for real users, URLs, or tokens. For documentation, refer to our
333: > relevant style guide sections on [fake user information](styleguide/_index.md#fake-user-information),
334: > [fake URLs](styleguide/_index.md#fake-urls), and [fake tokens](styleguide/_index.md#fake-tokens).
335: 
336: ### Simple cURL command
337: 
338: Get the details of a group:
339: 
340: ```shell
341: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
342:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups/gitlab-org"
343: ```
344: 
345: ### cURL example with parameters passed in the URL
346: 
347: Create a new project under the authenticated user's namespace:
348: 
349: ```shell
350: curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
351:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects?name=foo"
352: ```
353: 
354: ### Post data using cURL's `--data`
355: 
356: Instead of using `--request POST` and appending the parameters to the URI, you
357: can use cURL's `--data` option. The example below creates a new project
358: `foo` under the authenticated user's namespace.
359: 
360: ```shell
361: curl --data "name=foo" \
362:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
363:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects"
364: ```
365: 
366: ### Post data using cURL's `--data-urlencode`
367: 
368: Use `--data-urlencode` when the data contains special characters that require URL encoding.
369: 
370: You can use this option for:
371: 
372: - Markdown content with code blocks or special formatting.
373: - Regular expressions containing `+`, `.`, or `*`.
374: - Text with quotes, ampersands, or other reserved URL characters.
375: - File content that might contain special characters.
376: 
377: For alphanumeric data without special characters, use [`--data`](#post-data-using-curls---data) instead.
378: 
379: For an attribute with special characters:
380: 
381: ```shell
382: curl --request POST \
383:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
384:   --data-urlencode "description=Fix issue with 'quotes' & ampersands" \
385:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/issues"
386: ```
387: 
388: For content with regular expression patterns:
389: 
390: ```shell
391: curl --request DELETE \
392:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
393:   --data-urlencode "name_regex_delete=dev-.+" \
394:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/5/registry/repositories/2/tags"
395: ```
396: 
397: For content from a file, use `attribute@filename`:
398: 
399: ```shell
400: curl --request POST \
401:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
402:   --data-urlencode "title=API documentation update" \
403:   --data-urlencode "content@content.md" \
404:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/wikis"
405: ```
406: 
407: ### Post data using JSON content
408: 
409: This example creates a new group. Be aware of the use of single (`'`) and double
410: (`"`) quotes.
411: 
412: ```shell
413: curl --request POST \
414:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
415:   --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
416:   --data '{"path": "my-group", "name": "My group"}' \
417:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups"
418: ```
419: 
420: For readability, you can also set up the `--data` by using the following format:
421: 
422: ```shell
423: curl --request POST \
424:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups" \
425:   --header "content-type: application/json" \
426:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
427:   --data '{
428:     "path": "my-group",
429:     "name": "My group"
430: }'
431: ```
432: 
433: ### Post data using form-data
434: 
435: Instead of using JSON or URL-encoding data, you can use `multipart/form-data` which
436: properly handles data encoding:
437: 
438: ```shell
439: curl --request POST \
440:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
441:   --form "title=ssh-key" \

Governs every endpoint page produced by the Technical Writing team.\n**Sources of grounding:** The in-house `restapidocs_combined_template.md` endpoint template, the [GitLab REST API documentation guidelines](../task_folder/references/gitlab_api_doc_styleguide.md) snapshot, and the findings recorded in `doc_audit_tracker.csv`.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Purpose and scope\n\nThis guide exists because TaskFlow's API documentation was historically written ad-hoc by individual developers. The 2025 documentation audit (`doc_audit_tracker.csv`) found that of 17 audited endpoint rows, 6 required full rewrites, 7 required updates, and only 4 were acceptable as-is. The most common failure modes were not factual errors but *inconsistency*: two reviewers described the same object with different words (\"user\" vs. \"assignee\"), three different formatting styles were used for the same kind of information (tables, bullets, prose), and six pages drifted between active and passive voice.\n\nThis guide eliminates those failures by fixing a single canonical pattern for every endpoint page. If a rule here conflicts with an individual author's preference, this guide wins. If a rule here conflicts with verified product behavior, product behavior wins and this guide must be amended.\n\n## 2. Source-of-truth hierarchy\n\nTaskFlow documents one API from several sources. When sources disagree, resolve them in this order:\n\n1. **The OpenAPI specification** (`taskflow_openapi_v2_extract.yaml`) is the machine-readable contract extracted from the codebase. Parameter names, types, enums, defaults, requiredness, and declared status codes come from the spec.\n2. **Verified production behavior** (delivery logs, trace captures) is authoritative for behavior the spec does not model, such as webhook retry policy. Never publish production-derived behavior without labeling its provenance.\n3. **Prose documentation** is the presentation layer. It may add context, examples, and warnings, but it must never contradict the spec. Any docs-only claim (for example, \"tasks are created in the user's default project when `project_id` is omitted\") that is not backed by the spec must be tagged for engineering verification before publication.\n4. **The audit tracker** is a quality-control instrument, not a source of truth. Its notes reveal gaps that a plain diff of spec versus docs cannot (terminology drift, missing examples, inconsistent formatting). Every row must reach `acceptable` status before the docs it describes may ship.\n\nRule of engagement: **docs may say more than the spec, never less and never differently.** If the spec knows something the docs do not, that is a documentation bug. If the docs know something the spec does not, file a spec-backfill ticket (see §15).\n\n## 3. Page structure\n\nEvery endpoint page follows the combined template's skeleton, hardened with GitLab-style attribute tables. The mandatory order is:\n\n1. **H2 resource section** (for example, `## Tasks`) opening with the sentence pattern `Use this API to <verb> <feature>…`, per the GitLab introduction convention. Example: *\"Use this API to create, read, update, and delete tasks, the primary work units in TaskFlow.\"*\n2. **H3 operation section** per HTTP method. Each operation contains, in order:\n   - Operation title (see §4).\n   - A method-and-path block in a fenced `plaintext` code block, path always beginning with `/`:\n     ```plaintext\n     POST /api/v2/tasks\n     ```\n   - One-sentence description whose first sentence broadly restates the title (GitLab convention: \"List all tasks\" → \"Lists all tasks.\").\n   - Request attributes table (path parameters first, then query/body; required attributes first, then alphabetical). See §5.\n   - Success statement and response attributes, if the response body carries meaningful fields.\n   - Example request (cURL).\n   - Example response (JSON).\n   - Error table.\n3. **Cross-cutting H2 sections** collected once, not repeated per endpoint: Authentication, Rate limiting, Pagination, Errors, Timestamps and formats, Webhook delivery guarantees.\n\nThe page index must list every operation in the form used by the combined template — `* [Operation title](anchor) : `METHOD /path`` — grouped into *Open endpoints* (no auth) and *Endpoints that require authentication*, so readers can orient before diving in.\n\n## 4. Operation titles\n\nStart every operation title with the canonical verb for its HTTP method (adapted from GitLab):\n\n| HTTP method | Verb | Alternatives (use sparingly) | Example |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `GET` (multiple) | List | | **List tasks** |\n| `GET` (single) | Retrieve | Get | **Retrieve a task** |\n| `POST` | Create | Add | **Create a task** |\n| `PUT` | Update | Replace | **Update a task** |\n| `DELETE` | Delete | | **Delete a task** |\n\nForbidden constructions: headings phrased as sentences (\"Updating a task — PUT …\"), gerunds (\"Getting your profile\"), and synonyms that drift by page. Every operation below conforms to the [TaskFlow API Documentation Style Guide](taskflow_api_style_guide.md); parameters, enums, defaults, and status codes are reconciled against the OpenAPI 3.0 specification (v2.0.1) extracted from the codebase.\n\n## Endpoint index\n\n### Open endpoints\n\n* [Authenticate a user](#authenticate-a-user) : `POST /auth/login`\n* [Refresh an access token](#refresh-an-access-token) : `POST /auth/refresh`\n\n### Endpoints that require authentication\n\n#### Task related\n\n* [List tasks](#list-tasks) : `GET /tasks`\n* [Create a task](#create-a-task) : `POST /tasks`\n* [Retrieve a task](#retrieve-a-task) : `GET /tasks/{taskId}`\n* [Update a task](#update-a-task) : `PUT /tasks/{taskId}`\n* [Delete a task](#delete-a-task) : `DELETE /tasks/{taskId}`\n* [Assign a task](#assign-a-task) : `POST /tasks/{taskId}/assign`\n\n#### Project related\n\n* [List projects](#list-projects) : `GET /projects`\n* [Create a project](#create-a-project) : `POST /projects`\n* [Retrieve a project](#retrieve-a-project) : `GET /projects/{projectId}`\n* [Update a project](#update-a-project) : `PUT /projects/{projectId}`\n* [Delete a project](#delete-a-project) : `DELETE /projects/{projectId}`\n\n#### User related\n\n* [Retrieve the current user](#retrieve-the-current-user) : `GET /users/me`\n\n#### Webhook related\n\n* [Create a webhook](#create-a-webhook) : `POST /webhooks`\n* [Delete a webhook](#delete-a-webhook) : `DELETE /webhooks/{webhookId}`\n\n#### Search related\n\n* [Search tasks](#search-tasks) : `GET /search/tasks`\n\n---\n\n## Authentication\n\nTaskFlow v2 supports two credential types. Include either one in the `Authorization` header of every request to a protected endpoint:\n\n```plaintext\nAuthorization: Bearer <your_api_token>\n```\n\n1. **Static API tokens.** Generate a long-lived API token from the TaskFlow dashboard under **Settings > API Keys**. Use these for server-to-server integrations that do not act on behalf of an individual user.\n2. **Login token pairs.** Exchange a user's credentials for an access token and a refresh token with [`POST /auth/login`](#authenticate-a-user). Access tokens are short-lived; renew them with [`POST /auth/refresh`](#refresh-an-access-token). Use these for integrations that act on behalf of a user.\n\nIf credentials are missing, malformed, or expired, the API returns `401 Unauthorized` in the [standard error format](#errors).\n\n### Authenticate a user\n\nExchanges an email address and password for an access token and refresh token.\n\n```plaintext\nPOST /api/v2/auth/login\n```\n\nSupported attributes:\n\n| Attribute    | Type   | Required | Description                                                                 |\n|--------------|--------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `email`      | string | Yes      | The user's email address.                                                   |\n| `password`   | string | Yes      | The user's password.                                                        |\n| `mfa_code`   | string | Conditional | Time-based one-time code. Required if MFA is enabled on the account.     |\n\nIf successful, returns `200 OK` with a token pair:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"access_token\": \"at_9f2c...\",\n  \"refresh_token\": \"rt_1a8e...\",\n  \"token_type\": \"Bearer\",\n  \"expires_in\": 3600\n}\n```\n\n**Errors**\n\n| Status code | Meaning              | Common causes                                                        |\n|-------------|----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `401`       | Invalid credentials  | Unknown email, wrong password.                                       |\n| `403`       | MFA required         | MFA is enabled on the account and `mfa_code` was absent or invalid.  |\n\n### Refresh an access token\n\nExchanges a valid refresh token for a new token pair.\n\n```plaintext\nPOST /api/v2/auth/refresh\n```\n\nSupported attributes:\n\n| Attribute       | Type   | Required | Description                          |\n|-----------------|--------|----------|--------------------------------------|\n| `refresh_token` | string | Yes      | The refresh token issued by login.   |\n\nIf successful, returns `200 OK` and a new token pair (same shape as the login response).\n\n**Errors**\n\n| Status code | Meaning                             | Common causes                                    |\n|-------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|\n| `401`       | Refresh token expired or revoked    | Token older than its validity window, or rotated/revoked by logout. |\n\n---\n\n## Tasks\n\nUse this API to create, retrieve, update, and delete tasks, the primary work units in TaskFlow.\n\n### List tasks\n\nLists all tasks the authenticated user can access, with filtering, sorting, and pagination.\n\n```plaintext\nGET /api/v2/tasks\n```\n\nSupported attributes:\n\n| Attribute    | Type    | Required | Description                                                                        |\n|--------------|---------|----------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `status`     | string  | No       | Filter by task status. One of `open`, `in_progress`, `done`, `archived`, `blocked`.|\n| `project_id` | integer | No       | Only return tasks belonging to this project.                                       |\n| `page`       | integer | No       | Page number to return. |\n|---------------------|---------------|------------------------------------------|\n| `data`              | object array  | The page of task objects.                |\n| `data[].id`         |                         |\n| `data[].priority`   | string        | Task priority.                           |\n| `meta.current_page` | integer       | Page number returned.                    |\n| `meta.total_pages`  | integer       | Total number of pages available.         |\n| `meta.total_count`  | integer       | Total number of matching tasks.          |\n\nExample The payload lists exactly which fields changed via <code>changed_fields</code>.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"task.updated\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-01T15:05:33Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"task_id\": 1042,\n    \"changed_fields\": [\"status\", \"assignee_id\"],\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90002 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">task.assigned</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a task is assigned to an assignee, including reassignment to a different assignee.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A <code>POST /tasks/{taskId}/assign</code> request succeeds, or <code>assignee_id</code> is set via task update. Fires on the new assignment regardless of the <code>notify</code> flag (which controls email notification only).</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"task.assigned\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-05T10:02:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"task_id\": 1050,\n    \"assignee_id\": 93,\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90006 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">task.commented</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a comment is added to a task.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A comment is successfully attached to a task (UI or API).</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"task.commented\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-02T09:17:44Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"task_id\": 1042,\n    \"comment_id\": 5567,\n    \"actor_id\": 82\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90003 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">task.deleted</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a task is permanently deleted. Delivered after the deletion, so the referenced task no longer exists.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A <code>DELETE /tasks/{taskId}</code> request succeeds (204), or the containing project is deleted with <code>cascade=true</code>.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"task.deleted\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-08T09:00:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"task_id\": 999,\n    \"project_id\": 3,\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90010 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">task.due_date_approaching</span><span class=\"badge logonly\">Observed only</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Scheduled reminder that a task's due date is approaching. Not declared in the OpenAPI spec; not subscribable via <code>POST /webhooks</code> as specified.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>Daily scheduled check. Production evidence: fired at exactly <code>00:00:00Z</code> with <code>days_remaining: 9</code>, indicating a nightly job that fires when the task is within a fixed window of its due date.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"task.due_date_approaching\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-06T00:00:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"task_id\": 1042,\n    \"due_date\": \"2024-03-15T00:00:00Z\",\n    \"days_remaining\": 9\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge logonly\">Delivery d-90007 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">task.overdue</span><span class=\"badge logonly\">Observed only</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Scheduled notification that a task is past its due date. Not declared in the OpenAPI spec; not subscribable via <code>POST /webhooks</code> as specified.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>Daily scheduled check after midnight UTC once the due date has passed. Production evidence: fired at <code>00:00:00Z</code> with <code>days_overdue: 1</code>.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"task.overdue\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-16T00:00:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"task_id\": 1042,\n    \"due_date\": \"2024-03-15T00:00:00Z\",\n    \"days_overdue\": 1\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge logonly\">Delivery d-90011 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<h3 class=\"group\">Project events</h3>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">project.created</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a new project is created.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A <code>POST /projects</code> request succeeds (201), optionally from a <code>template_id</code>.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"project.created\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-09T13:55:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"project_id\": 15,\n    \"actor_id\": 82\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90012 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">project.archived</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a project is archived. Archived projects remain readable but leave active workflows.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A <code>PUT /projects/{projectId}</code> request sets <code>archived</code> to <code>true</code>.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"project.archived\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-03T11:30:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"project_id\": 8,\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90004 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">project.deleted</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a project is permanently deleted. With the default <code>cascade=true</code>, every task in the project is also deleted (each generating its own <code>task.deleted</code> event).</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A <code>DELETE /projects/{projectId}</code> request succeeds (204).</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"project.deleted\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-07T08:20:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"project_id\": 3,\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge logonly\">Delivery d-90008 — failed after 3 retries (HTTP 502, final_status: failed)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<h3 class=\"group\">Membership events</h3>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">member.added</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a user is added to a project with a role.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A membership is granted on a project (UI invite or API). The payload includes the granted role.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"member.added\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-04T16:45:12Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"project_id\": 12,\n    \"user_id\": 93,\n    \"role\": \"member\",\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90005 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">member.removed</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a user's membership on a project is removed.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A membership is revoked on a project (UI or API). Task assignments held by the removed member are not automatically reassigned.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"member.removed\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-07T14:10:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"project_id\": 12,\n    \"user_id\": 45,\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90009 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<h2>Observations from the delivery log</h2>\n<ul>\n  <li><strong>12 deliveries, 11 successful, 1 failed</strong> (<code>project.deleted</code>, HTTP 502, exhausted 3 retries).</li>\n  <li>All payload excerpts carry <code>actor_id</code> — the user who caused the event — except the two scheduled events (<code>task.due_date_approaching</code>, <code>task.overdue</code>), which are system-generated and have no actor.</li>\n  <li>Scheduled events fire at exactly <code>00:00:00Z</code>, consistent with a nightly batch job.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<footer>\n  TaskFlow Technical Writing · Sources: <code>taskflow_openapi_v2_extract.yaml</code> (declared events),\n  <code>webhook_delivery_log.json</code> (observed events), <code>doc_audit_tracker.csv</code> (retry-policy gap).\n  Payloads are reconstructed from production delivery excerpts; field order and envelope keys are illustrative.\n</footer>\n\n</main>\n</body>\n</html>\n","filePath":"/work/output/webhook_event_catalog.html"}", "type": "tool_call"}]}, {"role": "tool", "parts": [{"content": "Wrote file successfully.", "type": "text"}]}, {"role": "assistant", "parts": [{"content": "Now the migration guide:", "type": "text"}, {"content": "Now the migration guide. - Known issues/quirks (created Unix, last_login Unix, two error formats)", "type": "reasoning"}, {"id": "37acb02d-e78a-4163-97d5-89cd79c6d0cd", "name": "write", "arguments": "{"content":"# Migrating from TaskFlow API v1 to v2\n\n**Audience:** developers with integrations built against TaskFlow API v1 (`https://api.taskflow.io/api`).\n**Target version:** TaskFlow API v2.0.1 (`https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2`).\n**Related reading:** [TaskFlow API v2 Reference](taskflow_api_v2.md) · [Webhook Event Catalog](webhook_event_catalog.html)\n\nA v1 deprecation timeline has not yet been announced. Migrate at your convenience, but do not build new integrations on v1: v1 receives maintenance fixes only.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Breaking changes at a glance\n\n| Area | v1 | v2 | Action required |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Base URL | `https://api.taskflow.io/api` | `https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2` | Update every request |\n| Authentication | `X-API-Key: <key>` header | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | Change the header on every call |\n| Timestamps | Unix integers everywhere | ISO 8601 UTC (`2024-03-01T14:22:00Z`) | Change parsing/formatting; two legacy exceptions remain (§6) |\n| Pagination | `limit` / `offset` | `page` / `per_page` (default 25, max 200) | Rewrite paging logic |\n| List response shape | Bare JSON array | `data` array + `meta` object (tasks) | Update response parsing |\n| Task create success | `200 OK` | `201 Created` | Accept 201 |\n| Task assignment | `PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign` | `POST /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}/assign` | Change method and body field |\n| Task comments | `GET/POST /api/tasks/:id/comments` | `GET /tasks/{taskId}?include=comments` (read); no standalone write endpoint in v2 spec (§8) | Rework comment flows |\n| Task history | `GET /api/tasks/:id/history` | `GET /tasks/{taskId}?include=history` | Move to `include` |\n| Current user | `GET /api/users/current` | `GET /api/v2/users/me` | Update path; field renames |\n| Search | `GET /api/search` (tasks + projects) | `GET /api/v2/search/tasks` (tasks only) | Drop `type`; re-scope expectations |\n| Project delete | Always cascades | `cascade` query parameter, default `true` | Behavior-compatible; opt out with `cascade=false` |\n| Errors | `{\"error\": \"message\"}` | Structured `{\"error\": {\"code\", \"message\", \"details\"}}` (legacy format still appears on some endpoints) | Parse both during migration |\n| Rate limit | 60 requests/minute | 100/min (free), 1000/min (paid), `429` + `X-RateLimit-Remaining` | Handle 429; limits improved |\n| Webhook events | 4 event types | 10 declared event types (+2 observed in production) | Re-subscribe and verify handlers |\n\n## 2. Update the base URL and authentication\n\nReplace:\n\n```plaintext\nX-API-Key: <your_key>\nGET https://api.taskflow.io/api/tasks\n```\n\nwith:\n\n```bash\ncurl --header \"Authorization: Bearer <your_api_token>\" \\\n  --url \"https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks\"\n```\n\nYour existing dashboard API key continues to work as a Bearer token. If your integration acts on behalf of individual users, switch to the new token flow:\n\n1. `POST /api/v2/auth/login` with `email` and `password` (plus `mfa_code` if the account has MFA enabled) → returns `access_token` and `refresh_token`.\n2. Send `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on subsequent calls.\n3. When the access token expires, call `POST /api/v2/auth/refresh` with the `refresh_token` to obtain a new pair. A `401` from refresh means the token expired or was revoked — re-authenticate.\n\n## 3. Rename request fields\n\nv2 normalized several v1 field names. These renames apply to request and response bodies:\n\n| Object | v1 field | v2 field |\n|---|---|---|\n| Task | `desc` | `description` |\n| Task | `assigned_to` | `assignee_id` |\n| Task | `project` | `project_id` |\n| Task | `deadline` (Unix timestamp) | `due_date` (ISO 8601 date-time) |\n| Task assignment | `user_id` | `assignee_id` |\n| Project | `desc` | `description` |\n| User | `org` | `organization_id` |\n\nNew optional fields you can adopt immediately: `tags` and `watchers` on task create/update, `template_id` and `visibility` on project create, `notify` on task assignment, `secret` and `active` on webhook create.\n\n## 4. Convert timestamps\n\nv1 used Unix timestamps for all dates. v2 uses ISO 8601 UTC strings with a trailing `Z`.\n\n```text\nv1: \"deadline\": 1711929600        →  v2: \"due_date\": \"2024-04-01T00:00:00Z\"\nv1: history entry \"when\": 1709312400 →  v2: \"created_at\": \"2024-03-01T14:22:00Z\"\n```\n\nTwo documented v2 fields are still Unix timestamps — handle them explicitly:\n\n- Project object: `created` (Unix) — scheduled to migrate.\n- User object (`GET /users/me`): `last_login` (Unix) — `created_at` in the same object is already ISO 8601.\n\n## 5. Migrate pagination and list responses\n\n| v1 | v2 |\n|---|---|\n| `?limit=25&offset=50` | `?page=3&per_page=25` |\n| Response: `[ {...}, {...} ]` | Response: `{ \"data\": [ {...} ], \"meta\": { \"current_page\": 3, \"total_pages\": 5, \"total_count\": 98 } }` |\n\nNotes:\n\n- `per_page` defaults to 25 and caps at 200 on the tasks endpoint; the v1 default of 20 no longer applies.\n- Task list filters gain `blocked` as a status value, a `label` filter, and `due_date` as a sort field.\n- The projects list is now paginated in v2 (it accepts `page`/`per_page`). The projects response still uses a `projects` array rather than the `data` envelope — parse per endpoint.\n\n## 6. Endpoint-by-endpoint mapping\n\n| v1 endpoint | v2 endpoint | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| `GET /api/tasks` | `GET /api/v2/tasks` | Params renamed (`project`→`project_id`, `limit`/`offset`→`page`/`per_page`); envelope changed |\n| `POST /api/tasks` | `POST /api/v2/tasks` | Returns `201`, field renames (§3), `due_date` is ISO 8601 |\n| `GET /api/tasks/:id` | `GET /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}` | Add `include=comments,history,attachments` to expand related resources |\n| `PUT /api/tasks/:id` | `PUT /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}` | Still partial updates; new `409 Conflict` on concurrent modification — add retry logic |\n| `DELETE /api/tasks/:id` | `DELETE /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}` | Returns `204 No Content`; permission model is now documented (admin/owner on the project, or the task's creator) |\n| `PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign` | `POST /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}/assign` | Method changed PUT→POST; body `user_id`→`assignee_id`; optional `notify` (default `true`) |\n| `GET /api/tasks/:id/comments` | `GET /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}?include=comments` | See §8 |\n| `POST /api/tasks/:id/comments` | *No v2 equivalent in the current spec* | See §8 |\n| `GET /api/tasks/:id/history` | `GET /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}?include=history` | History timestamps are ISO 8601 in v2 |\n| `GET /api/projects` | `GET /api/v2/projects` | Adds `archived`, `role` (now including `viewer`), pagination |\n| `POST /api/projects` | `POST /api/v2/projects` | `desc`→`description`; adds `template_id`, `visibility` |\n| `DELETE /api/projects/:id` | `DELETE /api/v2/projects/{projectId}` | Same cascade behavior by default; `cascade=false` preserves tasks |\n| `GET /api/users/current` | `GET /api/v2/users/me` | `org`→`organization_id`; adds `timezone`; supports `fields` filter |\n| `GET /api/search` | `GET /api/v2/search/tasks` | Tasks only; `type` parameter removed; adds `project_id`, `status`, `date_from`, `date_to`; `q` is required |\n| `POST /api/webhooks` | `POST /api/v2/webhooks` | Event list expanded 4→10; adds `secret`, `active` (§7) |\n| `GET /api/webhooks` | *No v2 equivalent in the current spec* | Webhook listing is not exposed in v2; store webhook IDs at creation time |\n| `DELETE /api/webhooks/:id` | `DELETE /api/v2/webhooks/{webhookId}` | Returns `204 No Content` |\n\n## 7. Re-subscribe your webhooks\n\nv1 events were `task.created`, `task.updated`, `task.deleted`, `project.created`. All four still exist in v2 with the same names. The declared v2 enum adds six subscribable types:\n\n`task.assigned`, `task.commented`, `project.archived`, `project.deleted`, `member.added`, `member.removed`\n\nProduction also emits two scheduled event types that are **not** yet declared in the OpenAPI spec and therefore cannot be subscribed to via `POST /webhooks`: `task.due_date_approaching` and `task.overdue`. See the [Webhook Event Catalog](webhook_event_catalog.html) for descriptions, trigger conditions, payloads, and provenance for all twelve.\n\nOther webhook changes:\n\n- Provide a `secret` to receive HMAC-verifiable payloads; verify the signature against the raw body.\n- Delivery retry policy: up to 3 retries, then the delivery is marked `failed`.\n- Set `active: false` to pause a webhook without deleting it.\n\n## 8. Capabilities with no direct v2 equivalent\n\nPlan around these gaps:\n\n1. **Posting task comments** (`POST /api/tasks/:id/comments`) has no standalone v2 endpoint in the current OpenAPI spec. Reading comments is covered by `include=comments`. If you post comments via the API, keep the v1 call working until a v2 endpoint ships, or move comment creation into the UI. (A `task.commented` webhook event exists, confirming comment support in the platform.)\n2. **Listing webhooks** (`GET /api/webhooks`) is not exposed in v2. Persist your `webhook_id` values when you create webhooks so you can delete them later.\n3. **Project search** is gone: `GET /api/search?type=project` has no v2 counterpart because search is task-scoped. Track project membership client-side or via the `member.*` webhook events.\n\n## 9. Parse the new error format\n\nv2's canonical error body is structured:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"error\": {\n    \"code\": \"VALIDATION_ERROR\",\n    \"message\": \"Title is required\",\n    \"details\": []\n  }\n}\n```\n\nSome endpoints still return the legacy v1-style shape:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"error\": \"not_found\",\n  \"message\": \"Task not found\"\n}\n```\n\nWrite a parser that accepts both: if `error` is an object, read `error.code` and `error.message`; if it is a string, read the sibling `message`. The legacy format is transitional and will be removed.\n\n## 10. Migration checklist\n\n1. Update base URL to `https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2` everywhere.\n2. Replace the `X-API-Key` header with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; if you adopt the login flow, implement refresh-on-401 and MFA handling.\n3. Rename fields: `desc`, `assigned_to`, `project`, `deadline`, `user_id`, `org` (§3).\n4. Convert Unix timestamps to ISO 8601 on send; parse ISO 8601 on receive, with explicit handling for project `created` and user `last_login` (§4).\n5. Switch pagination to `page`/`per_page` and unwrap the `data`/`meta` envelope on the tasks list.\n6. Expect `201 Created` (not `200 OK`) from task and project creation, and `204 No Content` from deletions.\n7. Change task assignment from `PUT .../assign` to `POST .../assign` with `assignee_id`.\n8. Move comment and history reads to `?include=`; plan for the missing comment-write endpoint (§8).\n9. Handle `409 Conflict` on task updates with a re-fetch-and-retry loop.\n10. Make `DELETE /projects/{id}` explicit about `cascade` for your safety posture.\n11. Update search calls to `GET /search/tasks` and remove the `type` parameter.\n12. 1: # TaskFlow API Documentation
2: 
3: **Version**: 2.0
4: **Last Updated**: March 2024
5: 
6: Welcome to the TaskFlow API! This document describes how to interact with our REST API for managing tasks and projects. You can use these endpoints to build integrations with TaskFlow.
7: 
8: ## Authentication
9: 
10: All API calls require a valid API key. Include your key in the `Authorization` header:
11: 
12: ```
13: Authorization: Bearer <your_api_key>
14: ```
15: 
16: You can generate an API key from the TaskFlow dashboard under Settings > API Keys.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## Tasks
21: 
22: ### GET /api/v2/tasks
23: 
24: Retrieves a list of tasks for the authenticated user. The user can filter results using query parameters.
25: 
26: **Query Parameters**
27: 
28: | Parameter | Type | Description |
29: |-----------|------|-------------|
30: | status | string | Filter by task status. Allowed values: `open`, `in_progress`, `done`, `archived` |
31: | project_id | integer | Only return tasks belonging to this project |
32: | page | integer | Page number for pagination (default: 1) |
33: | per_page | integer | Number of results per page (default: 20, max: 100) |
34: | sort | string | Sort field. One of `created_at`, `updated_at`, `priority` |
35: | order | string | Sort direction: `asc` or `desc` |
36: 
37: **Example Request**
38: 
39: ```bash
40: curl -X GET "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks?status=open&page=1" \
41:   -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"
42: ```
43: 
44: **Response** (200 OK)
45: 
46: ```json
47: {
48:   "data": [
49:     {
50:       "id": 1042,
51:       "title": "Fix login bug",
52:       "description": "Users are unable to login with SSO",
53:       "status": "open",
54:       "priority": "high",
55:       "assignee_id": 57,
56:       "project_id": 12,
57:       "created_at": "2024-03-01T14:22:00Z",
58:       "updated_at": "2024-03-01T14:22:00Z",
59:       "due_date": "2024-03-15T00:00:00Z"
60:     }
61:   ],
62:   "meta": {
63:     "current_page": 1,
64:     "total_pages": 5,
65:     "total_count": 98
66:   }
67: }
68: ```
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ### POST /api/v2/tasks
73: 
74: Creates a new task. You must provide at least a title. The task will be created under the user's default project if `project_id` is not specified.
75: 
76: **Request Body Arguments**
77: 
78: - `title` (string, **required**) - The title of the task. Max 255 characters.
79: - `description` (string) - A longer description. Supports Markdown formatting.
80: - `status` (string) - Initial status. Defaults to `open`.
81: - `priority` (string) - One of: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`. Default is `medium`.
82: - `assignee_id` (integer) - User ID to assign the task to.
83: - `project_id` (integer) - Project to create the task in.
84: - `due_date` (string) - Due date in ISO 8601 format.
85: - `tags` (array of strings) - Tags to apply to the task.
86: 
87: **Example**
88: 
89: ```python
90: import requests
91: 
92: resp = requests.post(
93:     "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks",
94:     headers={"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"},
95:     json={
96:         "title": "Design new landing page",
97:         "description": "Create mockups for the Q2 marketing campaign",
98:         "priority": "high",
99:         "project_id": 12,
100:         "due_date": "2024-04-01T00:00:00Z",
101:         "tags": ["design", "marketing"]
102:     }
103: )
104: print(resp.json())
105: ```
106: 
107: Returns `201 Created` on success with the full task object in the response body.
108: 
109: **Errors**
110: 
111: | Status Code | Meaning |
112: |------------|---------|
113: | 400 | Bad request - missing required fields or invalid values |
114: | 401 | Authentication failed |
115: | 422 | Validation error (e.g. title too long) |
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ### GET /api/v2/tasks/{id}
120: 
121: Get a single task by its ID.
122: 
123: Pass the task ID as a path parameter. Returns the task object if found. Returns 404 if the task doesn't exist or you don't have access.
124: 
125: Response includes the full task object (same schema as list endpoint).
126: 
127: No additional arguments.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: ### Updating a task - PUT /api/v2/tasks/{id}
132: 
133: We support partial updates - you only need to send the fields you want to change. Any fields not included in the request body will remain unchanged.
134: 
135: Note: the `id` and `created_at` fields cannot be modified.
136: 
137: **Fields you can update:**
138: 
139: - title
140: - description
141: - status (must be a valid status string)
142: - priority
143: - assignee_id (set to `null` to unassign)
144: - project_id
145: - due_date (ISO 8601 timestamp or null to clear)
146: - tags
147: 
148: **Sample curl command:**
149: 
150: ```bash
151: curl -X PUT "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks/1042" \
152:   -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
153:   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
154:   -d '{"status": "in_progress", "assignee_id": 57}'
155: ```
156: 
157: The API returns `200 OK` and the updated task object on success.
158: 
159: ---
160: 
161: ### DELETE /api/v2/tasks/{id}
162: 
163: Permanently deletes a task. This action cannot be undone.
164: 
165: The user must have admin or owner permissions on the project that the task belongs to. Regular members can only delete tasks they created.
166: 
167: **Returns:**
168: 
169: `204 No Content` on success. The response body is empty.
170: 
171: If the task is not found a `404` error is returned. Attempting to delete a task without sufficient permissions results in `403 Forbidden`.
172: 
173: ---
174: 
175: ## Projects
176: 
177: ### List projects
178: 
179: ```
180: GET /api/v2/projects
181: ```
182: 
183: This route returns all projects the authenticated user has access to. Projects are returned in alphabetical order by name.
184: 
185: **Query args:**
186: 
187: - `archived` (boolean) - if `true`, include archived projects. Default `false`.
188: - `role` (string) - filter by the user's role in the project: `owner`, `admin`, `member`
189: 
190: No authentication header examples are given here since it follows the same pattern described at the top of this doc.
191: 
192: **Sample response:**
193: 
194: ```json
195: {
196:   "projects": [
197:     {
198:       "id": 12,
199:       "name": "Website Redesign",
200:       "description": "Q2 2024 website overhaul",
201:       "owner_id": 57,
202:       "created": 1709312400,
203:       "member_count": 8,
204:       "task_count": 45,
205:       "archived": false
206:     }
207:   ]
208: }
209: ```
210: 
211: Note that the `created` field here returns a Unix timestamp. We plan to migrate this to ISO 8601 in a future release.
212: 
213: ---
214: 
215: ### Create Project
216: 
217: **Endpoint:** `POST /api/v2/projects`
218: 
219: To create a new project, send a POST request with the following payload:
220: 
221: ```json
222: {
223:   "name": "My New Project",
224:   "description": "Optional project description"
225: }
226: ```
227: 
228: The `name` field is required and must be unique within the user's organization. Max 100 chars.
229: 
230: **Response fields:**
231: 
232: | Field | Type | Notes |
233: |-------|------|-------|
234: | id | integer | Auto-generated project ID |
235: | name | string | The project name |
236: | description | string | May be null |
237: | owner_id | integer | ID of creating user |
238: | created | integer | Unix timestamp |
239: | member_count | integer | Always 1 for new projects |
240: | task_count | integer | Always 0 for new projects |
241: | archived | boolean | Always false for new projects |
242: 
243: Returns HTTP 201.
244: 
245: No error documentation is provided here but the API follows standard REST conventions for error responses.
246: 
247: ---
248: 
249: ## User Info
250: 
251: ### Getting your profile
252: 
253: **Route**: GET /api/v2/users/me
254: 
255: This returns information about the currently authenticated user. Pass your API key as usual.
256: 
257: The response looks like:
258: 
259: ```json
260: {
261:   "user": {
262:     "id": 57,
263:     "email": "jane@example.com",
264:     "name": "Jane Smith",
265:     "role": "admin",
266:     "organization_id": 5,
267:     "timezone": "America/New_York",
268:     "created_at": "2023-01-15T09:00:00Z",
269:     "last_login": 1709398800
270:   }
271: }
272: ```
273: 
274: Note: `created_at` is ISO 8601 but `last_login` is a Unix timestamp. This inconsistency will be addressed in API v3.
275: 
276: ---
277: 
278: ## Rate Limiting
279: 
280: We enforce rate limits to ensure fair usage of the API. The current limits are:
281: 
282: - 100 requests per minute for free tier
283: - 1000 requests per minute for paid plans
284: 
285: When you exceed the limit, the API returns `429 Too Many Requests`. Check the `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header to see how many requests you have left.
286: 
287: ## Pagination
288: 
289: List endpoints support pagination via `page` and `per_page` query parameters. The response `meta` object contains pagination info. Note that the projects endpoint does not currently support pagination - all projects are returned in a single response.
290: 
291: ## Errors
292: 
293: The API uses standard HTTP status codes. Error responses include a JSON body:
294: 
295: ```json
296: {
297:   "error": {
298:     "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
299:     "message": "Title is required",
300:     "details": []
301:   }
302: }
303: ```
304: 
305: However, some older endpoints may return errors in a different format:
306: 
307: ```json
308: {
309:   "error": "not_found",
310:   "message": "Task not found"
311: }
312: ```
313: 
314: We are working on standardizing error responses across all routes.
315: 
316: ---
317: 
318: *For questions or support, email api-support@taskflow.io*

1: # TaskFlow API v1
2: 
3: API base URL: `https://api.taskflow.io/api`
4: 
5: Auth: use `X-API-Key` header with your key.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## GET /api/tasks
10: 
11: Gets tasks. Returns JSON array.
12: 
13: Params: `status`, `project`, `limit`, `offset`
14: 
15: Response: array of task objects.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## POST /api/tasks
20: 
21: Create a task.
22: 
23: Body: JSON with `title` (required), `desc`, `status`, `priority`, `assigned_to`, `project`, `deadline`.
24: 
25: `deadline` should be a Unix timestamp.
26: 
27: Returns the created task. 200 OK.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## GET /api/tasks/:id
32: 
33: Fetch one task.
34: 
35: ---
36: 
37: ## PUT /api/tasks/:id
38: 
39: Update task fields. Send only what changed.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## DELETE /api/tasks/:id
44: 
45: Delete a task. Must be owner.
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## GET /api/projects
50: 
51: List all projects.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## POST /api/projects
56: 
57: Make a new project. Body: `name` (required), `desc`.
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## GET /api/users/current
62: 
63: Get current user info.
64: 
65: Response:
66: 
67: ```
68: {
69:   "id": 57,
70:   "email": "jane@example.com",
71:   "name": "Jane Smith",
72:   "role": "admin",
73:   "org": 5
74: }
75: ```
76: 
77: ---
78: 
79: ## GET /api/tasks/:id/comments
80: 
81: List comments on a task.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## POST /api/tasks/:id/comments
86: 
87: Add comment. Body: `text`.
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ## GET /api/search
92: 
93: Search across tasks and projects.
94: 
95: Params: `q` (search query), `type` (task or project)
96: 
97: ---
98: 
99: ## PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign
100: 
101: Assign a task to a user. Body: `user_id`.
102: 
103: This is a convenience endpoint. You can also update the `assigned_to` field directly via PUT /api/tasks/:id.
104: 
105: ---
106: 
107: ## GET /api/tasks/:id/history
108: 
109: Returns change history for a task. Each entry shows what field changed, old value, new value, who changed it, and when (Unix timestamp).
110: 
111: ---
112: 
113: ## DELETE /api/projects/:id
114: 
115: Delete a project. All tasks in the project will also be deleted.
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ## Errors
120: 
121: Errors return JSON: `{"error": "message"}`.
122: 
123: Common codes: 400, 401, 404, 500.
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## Webhooks
128: 
129: POST /api/webhooks - register a webhook. Body: `url`, `events` (array).
130: 
131: GET /api/webhooks - list webhooks.
132: 
133: DELETE /api/webhooks/:id - remove a webhook.
134: 
135: Events: `task.created`, `task.updated`, `task.deleted`, `project.created`.
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## Notes
140: 
141: - Rate limit: 60 req/min.
142: - All timestamps are Unix.
143: - Contact support@taskflow.io for help.

(End of file - total 143 lines)
</content>", "type": "text"}]

1: # RESTAPIDocs Examples
2: 
3: These examples were taken from projects mainly using [Django Rest
4: Framework](https://github.com/tomchristie/django-rest-framework) and so the
5: JSON responses are often similar to the way in which DRF makes responses.
6: 
7: Where full URLs are provided in responses they will be rendered as if service
8: is running on 'http://testserver/'.
9: 
10: ## Open Endpoints
11: 
12: Open endpoints require no Authentication.
13: 
14: * [Login](login.md) : `POST /api/login/`
15: 
16: ## Endpoints that require Authentication
17: 
18: Closed endpoints require a valid Token to be included in the header of the
19: request. A Token can be acquired from the Login view above.
20: 
21: ### Current User related
22: 
23: Each endpoint manipulates or displays information related to the User whose
24: Token is provided with the request:
25: 
26: * [Show info](user/get.md) : `GET /api/user/`
27: * [Update info](user/put.md) : `PUT /api/user/`
28: 
29: ### Account related
30: 
31: Endpoints for viewing and manipulating the Accounts that the Authenticated User
32: has permissions to access.
33: 
34: * [Show Accessible Accounts](accounts/get.md) : `GET /api/accounts/`
35: * [Create Account](accounts/post.md) : `POST /api/accounts/`
36: * [Show An Account](accounts/pk/get.md) : `GET /api/accounts/:pk/`
37: * [Update An Account](accounts/pk/put.md) : `PUT /api/accounts/:pk/`
38: * [Delete An Account](accounts/pk/delete.md) : `DELETE /api/accounts/:pk/`
39: # Show Current User
40: 
41: Get the details of the currently Authenticated User along with basic
42: subscription information.
43: 
44: **URL** : `/api/user/`
45: 
46: **Method** : `GET`
47: 
48: **Auth required** : YES
49: 
50: **Permissions required** : None
51: 
52: ## Success Response
53: 
54: **Code** : `200 OK`
55: 
56: **Content examples**
57: 
58: For a User with ID 1234 on the local database where that User has saved an
59: email address and name information.
60: 
61: ```json
62: {
63:     "id": 1234,
64:     "first_name": "Joe",
65:     "last_name": "Bloggs",
66:     "email": "joe25@example.com"
67: }
68: ```
69: 
70: For a user with ID 4321 on the local database but no details have been set yet.
71: 
72: ```json
73: {
74:     "id": 4321,
75:     "first_name": "",
76:     "last_name": "",
77:     "email": ""
78: }
79: ```
80: 
81: ## Notes
82: 
83: * If the User does not have a `UserInfo` instance when requested then one will
84:   be created for them.
85: 404: Not Found404: Not Found404: Not Found404: Not Found

1: ---
2: stage: none
3: group: unassigned
4: info: For assistance with this Style Guide page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments-to-other-projects-and-subjects>.
5: description: Writing styles, markup, formatting, and other standards for the GitLab RESTful APIs.
6: title: Documenting REST API resources
7: ---
8: 
9: REST API resources are documented in Markdown under
10: [`/doc/api`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api). Each
11: resource has its own Markdown file, which is linked from
12: [`api_resources.md`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/doc/api/api_resources.md).
13: 
14: When modifying the Markdown or API code, also update the corresponding
15: [OpenAPI definition](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api/openapi), by running
16: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:generate` and `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:generate`.
17: To check if the OpenAPI definition needs to be updated, you can run `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:check_docs` and
18: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:check_docs`.
19: This is also checked by the `openapi-doc-check` CI/CD job that runs for commits that modify API code or documentation.
20: 
21: The Markdown topic for an API resource must include:
22: 
23: - A block that includes the HTTP method (like GET, PUT, DELETE) followed by the request path. Always start the path with a `/`. For example:
24: 
25:   ```plaintext
26:   GET /api/v4/projects/:id/repository/branches
27:   ```
28: 
29: - A detailed [description of the attributes](#request-attributes).
30: - A detailed [description of the response body](#response-attributes).
31: - A cURL example.
32: - A response body example (in JSON format).
33: 
34: After a new API documentation page is added, [add an entry in the global navigation](site_architecture/global_nav.md#add-a-navigation-entry).
35: 
36: ## Page metadata
37: 
38: When you create a new page, include a `description` metadata field
39: in the front matter that follows these guidelines for consistency:
40: 
41: - Start with "REST API to"
42: - Use action verbs that describe what users can do with the API
43: - Avoid words ending in -ing
44: - Keep to one sentence, ideally under 100 characters
45: - End with a period
46: 
47: For example:
48: 
49: ```yaml
50: ---
51: stage: Example Stage
52: group: Example Group
53: info: To determine the technical writer assigned to the Stage/Group associated with this page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments>
54: description: REST API to create, update, and delete issues.
55: title: Example page title
56: ---
57: ```
58: 
59: Additional examples:
60: 
61: - `description: REST API to retrieve CI/CD job details, retry and cancel jobs, run manual jobs, and access job logs.`
62: - `description: REST API to create, manage, and monitor CI/CD pipelines.`
63: 
64: ## API topic template
65: 
66: Use the following template to help you get started. Be sure to list any
67: required attributes first in the table.
68: 
69: ````markdown
70: ## API name
71: 
72: {{</* history */>}}
73: 
74: - History note.
75: 
76: {{</* /history */>}}
77: 
78: Use this API to ...
79: 
80: ### Operation title
81: 
82: {{</* history */>}}
83: 
84: - History note.
85: 
86: {{</* /history */>}}
87: 
88: Description of the operation.
89: 
90: ```plaintext
91: METHOD /api/v4/endpoint
92: ```
93: 
94: Supported attributes:
95: 
96: | Attribute                | Type     | Required | Description           |
97: |--------------------------|----------|----------|-----------------------|
98: | `attribute`              | datatype | Yes      | Detailed description. |
99: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
100: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
101: | `attribute`              | datatype | No       | Detailed description. |
102: 
103: If successful, returns [`<status_code>`](rest/troubleshooting.md#status-codes) and the following
104: response attributes:
105: 
106: | Attribute                | Type     | Description           |
107: |--------------------------|----------|-----------------------|
108: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
109: | `attribute`              | datatype | Detailed description. |
110: 
111: Example request:
112: 
113: ```shell
114: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
115:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/endpoint?parameters"
116: ```
117: 
118: Example response:
119: 
120: ```json
121: [
122:   {
123:   }
124: ]
125: ```
126: ````
127: 
128: ## History
129: 
130: Add [history](styleguide/availability_details.md#history)
131: to describe new or updated API calls.
132: 
133: To add history for an individual attribute, include it in the history
134: for the section. For example:
135: 
136: ```markdown
137: ### Edit a widget
138: 
139: {{</* history */>}}
140: 
141:  - `widget_message` [introduced](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.3.
142: 
143: {{</* /history */>}}
144: ```
145: 
146: If the API or attribute is deployed behind a feature flag,
147: [include the feature flag information](feature_flags.md) in the history.
148: 
149: ## Deprecations
150: 
151: To document the deprecation of an API endpoint, follow the steps to
152: [deprecate a page or topic](styleguide/deprecations_and_removals.md).
153: 
154: To deprecate an attribute:
155: 
156: 1. Add a history note.
157: 
158:    ```markdown
159:    {{</* history */>}}
160: 
161:    - `widget_name` [deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7.
162: 
163:    {{</* /history */>}}
164:    ```
165: 
166: 1. Add inline deprecation text to the description.
167: 
168:    ```markdown
169:    | Attribute     | Type   | Required | Description |
170:    |---------------|--------|----------|-------------|
171:    | `widget_name` | string | No       | [Deprecated](https://link-to-issue) in GitLab 14.7. Use `widget_id` instead. The name of the widget. |
172:    ```
173: 
174: To widely announce a deprecation, [update the REST API deprecations page](../../api/rest/deprecations.md).
175: 
176: ## API introduction
177: 
178: Each API is made of one or more operations. At the start of the topic, include information that
179: applies to all operations in the API, and a short description of the related features.
180: 
181: For consistency, try to start the introduction with: `Use this API to {verb} + [{feature}](link/to/UI/docs).`
182: This allows us to direct users to related documentation that might include more context.
183: 
184: For example:
185: 
186: - `Use this API to manage [Git branches](path/to/file).`
187: - `Use this API to interact with the [Maven package manager client](path/to/file).`
188: - `Use this API to interact with namespaces, a special resource category used to organize users and groups. For more information, see [namespaces](path/to/file).`
189: 
190: ## Operation titles
191: 
192: Start an operation title with a verb. For consistency,
193: use these verbs based on the HTTP method:
194: 
195: | HTTP method      | Verb     | Alternatives | Examples |
196: | ---------------- | -------- | ------------ | -------- |
197: | `GET` (multiple) | List all |              | `List all group access tokens` |
198: | `GET` (single)   | Retrieve | Download     | `Retrieve a group audit event`, `Download a dependency list export` |
199: | `POST`           | Create   | Add          | `Create a repository branch`, `Add a new emoji reaction` |
200: | `PUT`            | Update   | Replace      | `Update a project topic` |
201: | `PATCH`          | Update   | Modify       | `Update a freeze period`, `Modify an existing commit thread note` |
202: | `DELETE`         | Delete   |              | `Delete a feature` |
203: 
204: When possible, use the recommended verb. Alternatives might be needed in specific contexts, but
205: minimize their use to maintain consistency.
206: 
207: ## Operation descriptions
208: 
209: Each operation should include a short description that explains its use, and highlights any
210: important information. If possible, write the first sentence to broadly repeat the title of
211: the operation. For example:
212: 
213: - `List all project access tokens` -> `Lists all project access tokens.`
214: - `Delete an SSH key` -> `Deletes an SSH key from your user account.`
215: - `Retrieve an enterprise user` -> `Retrieves details on a specified enterprise user.`
216: 
217: ## Request attributes
218: 
219: You must document the request attributes in an operation. When creating the table and attribute descriptions:
220: 
221: - Use the following column names for attribute tables.
222: - List any path attributes first, then any required attributes, then sort alphabetically.
223: - Place the attribute name in code blocks using backticks (`` ` ``).
224: - Document any tier or offering information specific to an attribute in the description.
225:   - If an attribute is available for Premium, mention that it's also available for Ultimate.
226:   - Combine this tier and offering information when possible. For example: `GitLab Self-Managed, Premium and Ultimate only.`
227: 
228: ```markdown
229: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
230: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
231: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
232: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
233: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
234: ```
235: 
236: Rendered example:
237: 
238: | Attribute                    | Type          | Required | Description                                         |
239: |------------------------------|---------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------|
240: | `title`                      | string        | Yes      | Title of the issue. GitLab Self-Managed only.       |
241: | `assignee_ids`               | integer array | No       | IDs of the users to assign the issue to. Ultimate only. |
242: | `confidential`               | boolean       | No       | Sets the issue to confidential. Default is `false`. |
243: 
244: For information about writing attribute descriptions, see the [GraphQL API description style guide](../api_graphql_styleguide.md#description-style-guide).
245: 
246: ### Conditionally required attributes
247: 
248: If an attribute is related to another item, indicate this in the attribute description.
249: 
250: Generally, this happens if one of two attributes is required or if an attribute must be enabled and configured separately.
251: 
252: First define the attribute itself, then mention any requirements. Use this format:
253: 
254:   ```markdown
255:   Required if `attribute1` is `true`.
256:   ```
257: 
258: For example:
259: 
260: | Attribute                  | Type    | Required    | Description |
261: | -------------------------- | ------- | ----------- | ----------- |
262: | `include_saml_users`       | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns users with a SAML identity. Required if `include_service_accounts` is `false`. |
263: | `include_service_accounts` | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, returns service account users. Required if `include_saml_users` is `false`. |
264: | `a_related_setting`        | boolean | Conditional | If `true`, does something else. Required if `include_saml_users` is `true`. |
265: 
266: ## Response attributes

306: 
307: - Use `https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/` as an endpoint.
308: - Wherever needed use this personal access token: `<your_access_token>`.
309: - Always put the request first. `GET` is the default so you don't have to

312:   [`scripts/lint-doc.sh`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/scripts/lint-doc.sh).)
313: - Declare URLs with the `--url` parameter, and wrap the URL in double quotes (`"`).
314: - Prefer to use examples using the personal access token and don't pass data of
315:   username and password.
316: - For legibility, use the ` \ ` character and indentation to break long single-line
317:   commands apart into multiple lines.
318: 
319: | Methods                                         | Description                                            |
320: |-------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|

322: | `--request POST`                                | Use this method when creating new objects.             |
