With the default <code>cascade=true</code>, every task in the project is also deleted (each generating its own <code>task.deleted</code> event).</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A <code>DELETE /projects/{projectId}</code> request succeeds (204).</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"project.deleted\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-07T08:20:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"project_id\": 3,\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge logonly\">Delivery d-90008 — failed after 3 retries (HTTP 502, final_status: failed)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<h3 class=\"group\">Membership events</h3>\n\n<div class=\"card\">\n  <h4><span class=\"event-name\">member.added</span><span class=\"badge both\">Declared + observed</span></h4>\n  <dl>\n    <dt>Description</dt>\n    <dd>Fires when a user is added to a project with a role.</dd>\n    <dt>Trigger condition</dt>\n    <dd>A membership is granted on a project (UI invite or API). Task assignments held by the removed member are not automatically reassigned.</dd>\n    <dt>Example payload</dt>\n    <dd><pre><code>{\n  \"event\": \"member.removed\",\n  \"timestamp\": \"2024-03-07T14:10:00Z\",\n  \"webhook_id\": 301,\n  \"data\": {\n    \"project_id\": 12,\n    \"user_id\": 45,\n    \"actor_id\": 57\n  }\n}</code></pre>\n    <span class=\"badge spec\">Reconstructed from delivery d-90009 (HTTP 200)</span></dd>\n  </dl>\n</div>\n\n<h2>Observations from the delivery log</h2>\n<ul>\n  <li><strong>12 deliveries, 11 successful, 1 failed</strong> (<code>project.deleted</code>, HTTP 502, exhausted 3 retries).</li>\n  <li>All payload excerpts carry <code>actor_id</code> — the user who caused the event — except the two scheduled events (<code>task.due_date_approaching</code>, <code>task.overdue</code>), which are system-generated and have no actor.</li>\n  <li>Scheduled events fire at exactly <code>00:00:00Z</code>, consistent with a nightly batch job.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<footer>\n  TaskFlow Technical Writing · Sources: <code>taskflow_openapi_v2_extract.yaml</code> (declared events),\n  <code>webhook_delivery_log.json</code> (observed events), <code>doc_audit_tracker.csv</code> (retry-policy gap).\n  Payloads are reconstructed from production delivery excerpts; field order and envelope keys are illustrative.\n</footer>\n\n</main>\n</body>\n</html>\n","filePath":"/work/output/webhook_event_catalog.html"}", "type": "tool_call"}]}, {"role": "tool", "parts": [{"content": "Wrote file successfully.", "type": "text"}]}]}, "output": {"messages": [{"role": "assistant", "parts": [{"content": "Now the migration guide:", "type": "text"}, {"content": "Now the migration guide. Migrate at your convenience, but do not build new integrations on v1: v1 receives maintenance fixes only.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Breaking changes at a glance\n\n| Area | v1 | v2 | Action required |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Base URL | `https://api.taskflow.io/api` | `https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2` | Update every request |\n| Authentication | `X-API-Key: <key>` header | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | Change the header on every call |\n| Timestamps | Unix integers everywhere | ISO 8601 UTC (`2024-03-01T14:22:00Z`) | Change parsing/formatting; two legacy exceptions remain (§6) |\n| Pagination | `limit` / `offset` | `page` / `per_page` (default 25, max 200) | Rewrite paging logic |\n| List response shape | Bare JSON array | `data` array + `meta` object (tasks) | Update response parsing |\n| Task create success | `200 OK` | `201 Created` | Accept 201 |\n| Task assignment | `PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign` | `POST /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}/assign` | Change method and body field |\n| Task comments | `GET/POST /api/tasks/:id/comments` | `GET /tasks/{taskId}?include=comments` (read); no standalone write endpoint in v2 spec (§8) | Rework comment flows |\n| Task history | `GET /api/tasks/:id/history` | `GET /tasks/{taskId}?include=history` | Move to `include` |\n| Current user | `GET /api/users/current` | `GET /api/v2/users/me` | Update path; field renames |\n| Search | `GET /api/search` (tasks + projects) | `GET /api/v2/search/tasks` (tasks only) | Drop `type`; re-scope expectations |\n| Project delete | Always cascades | `cascade` query parameter, default `true` | Behavior-compatible; opt out with `cascade=false` |\n| Errors | `{\"error\": \"message\"}` | Structured `{\"error\": {\"code\", \"message\", \"details\"}}` (legacy format still appears on some endpoints) | Parse both during migration |\n| Rate limit | 60 requests/minute | 100/min (free), 1000/min (paid), `429` + `X-RateLimit-Remaining` | Handle 429; limits improved |\n| Webhook events | 4 event types | 10 declared event types (+2 observed in production) | Re-subscribe and verify handlers |\n\n## 2. Update the base URL and authentication\n\nReplace:\n\n```plaintext\nX-API-Key: <your_key>\nGET https://api.taskflow.io/api/tasks\n```\n\nwith:\n\n```bash\ncurl --header \"Authorization: Bearer <your_api_token>\" \\\n  --url \"https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks\"\n```\n\nYour existing dashboard API key continues to work as a Bearer token. If your integration acts on behalf of individual users, switch to the new token flow:\n\n1. `POST /api/v2/auth/login` with `email` and `password` (plus `mfa_code` if the account has MFA enabled) → returns `access_token` and `refresh_token`.\n2. Send `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on subsequent calls.\n3. When the access token expires, call `POST /api/v2/auth/refresh` with the `refresh_token` to obtain a new pair. A `401` from refresh means the token expired or was revoked — re-authenticate.\n\n## 3. Rename request fields\n\nv2 normalized several v1 field names. These renames apply to request and response bodies:\n\n| Object | v1 field | v2 field |\n|---|---|---|\n| Task | `desc` | `description` |\n| Task | `assigned_to` | `assignee_id` |\n| Task | `project` | `project_id` |\n| Task | `deadline` (Unix timestamp) | `due_date` (ISO 8601 date-time) |\n| Task assignment | `user_id` | `assignee_id` |\n| Project | `desc` | `description` |\n| User | `org` | `organization_id` |\n\nNew optional fields you can adopt immediately: `tags` and `watchers` on task create/update, `template_id` and `visibility` on project create, `notify` on task assignment, `secret` and `active` on webhook create.\n\n## 4. Convert timestamps\n\nv1 used Unix timestamps for all dates. v2 uses ISO 8601 UTC strings with a trailing `Z`.\n\n```text\nv1: \"deadline\": 1711929600        →  v2: \"due_date\": \"2024-04-01T00:00:00Z\"\nv1: history entry \"when\": 1709312400 →  v2: \"created_at\": \"2024-03-01T14:22:00Z\"\n```\n\nTwo documented v2 fields are still Unix timestamps — handle them explicitly:\n\n- Project object: `created` (Unix) — scheduled to migrate.\n- User object (`GET /users/me`): `last_login` (Unix) — `created_at` in the same object is already ISO 8601.\n\n## 5. Migrate pagination and list responses\n\n| v1 | v2 |\n|---|---|\n| `?limit=25&offset=50` | `?page=3&per_page=25` |\n| Response: `[ {...}, {...} ]` | Response: `{ \"data\": [ {...} ], \"meta\": { \"current_page\": 3, \"total_pages\": 5, \"total_count\": 98 } }` |\n\nNotes:\n\n- `per_page` defaults to 25 and caps at 200 on the tasks endpoint; the v1 default of 20 no longer applies.\n- Task list filters gain `blocked` as a status value, a `label` filter, and `due_date` as a sort field.\n- The projects list is now paginated in v2 (it accepts `page`/`per_page`). The projects response still uses a `projects` array rather than the `data` envelope — parse per endpoint.\n\n## 6. Endpoint-by-endpoint mapping\n\n| v1 endpoint | v2 endpoint | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| `GET /api/tasks` | `GET /api/v2/tasks` | Params renamed (`project`→`project_id`, `limit`/`offset`→`page`/`per_page`); envelope changed |\n| `POST /api/tasks` | `POST /api/v2/tasks` | Returns `201`, field renames (§3), `due_date` is ISO 8601 |\n| `GET /api/tasks/:id` | `GET /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}` | Add `include=comments,history,attachments` to expand related resources |\n| `PUT /api/tasks/:id` | `PUT /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}` | Still partial updates; new `409 Conflict` on concurrent modification — add retry logic |\n| `DELETE /api/tasks/:id` | `DELETE /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}` | Returns `204 No Content`; permission model is now documented (admin/owner on the project, or the task's creator) |\n| `PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign` | `POST /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}/assign` | Method changed PUT→POST; body `user_id`→`assignee_id`; optional `notify` (default `true`) |\n| `GET /api/tasks/:id/comments` | `GET /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}?include=comments` | See §8 |\n| `POST /api/tasks/:id/comments` | *No v2 equivalent in the current spec* | See §8 |\n| `GET /api/tasks/:id/history` | `GET /api/v2/tasks/{taskId}?include=history` | History timestamps are ISO 8601 in v2 |\n| `GET /api/projects` | `GET /api/v2/projects` | Adds `archived`, `role` (now including `viewer`), pagination |\n| `POST /api/projects` | `POST /api/v2/projects` | `desc`→`description`; adds `template_id`, `visibility` |\n| `DELETE /api/projects/:id` | `DELETE /api/v2/projects/{projectId}` | Same cascade behavior by default; `cascade=false` preserves tasks |\n| `GET /api/users/current` | `GET /api/v2/users/me` | `org`→`organization_id`; adds `timezone`; supports `fields` filter |\n| `GET /api/search` | `GET /api/v2/search/tasks` | Tasks only; `type` parameter removed; adds `project_id`, `status`, `date_from`, `date_to`; `q` is required |\n| `POST /api/webhooks` | `POST /api/v2/webhooks` | Event list expanded 4→10; adds `secret`, `active` (§7) |\n| `GET /api/webhooks` | *No v2 equivalent in the current spec* | Webhook listing is not exposed in v2; store webhook IDs at creation time |\n| `DELETE /api/webhooks/:id` | `DELETE /api/v2/webhooks/{webhookId}` | Returns `204 No Content` |\n\n## 7. Re-subscribe your webhooks\n\nv1 events were `task.created`, `task.updated`, `task.deleted`, `project.created`. All four still exist in v2 with the same names. The declared v2 enum adds six subscribable types:\n\n`task.assigned`, `task.commented`, `project.archived`, `project.deleted`, `member.added`, `member.removed`\n\nProduction also emits two scheduled event types that are **not** yet declared in the OpenAPI spec and therefore cannot be subscribed to via `POST /webhooks`: `task.due_date_approaching` and `task.overdue`. See the [Webhook Event Catalog](webhook_event_catalog.html) for descriptions, trigger conditions, payloads, and provenance for all twelve.\n\nOther webhook changes:\n\n- Provide a `secret` to receive HMAC-verifiable payloads; verify the signature against the raw body.\n- Delivery retry policy: up to 3 retries, then the delivery is marked `failed`.\n- Set `active: false` to pause a webhook without deleting it.\n\n## 8. Capabilities with no direct v2 equivalent\n\nPlan around these gaps:\n\n1. **Posting task comments** (`POST /api/tasks/:id/comments`) has no standalone v2 endpoint in the current OpenAPI spec. Reading comments is covered by `include=comments`. If you post comments via the API, keep the v1 call working until a v2 endpoint ships, or move comment creation into the UI. (A `task.commented` webhook event exists, confirming comment support in the platform.)\n2. **Listing webhooks** (`GET /api/webhooks`) is not exposed in v2. Persist your `webhook_id` values when you create webhooks so you can delete them later.\n3. **Project search** is gone: `GET /api/search?type=project` has no v2 counterpart because search is task-scoped. Track project membership client-side or via the `member.*` webhook events.\n\n## 9. Parse the new error format\n\nv2's canonical error body is structured:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"error\": {\n    \"code\": \"VALIDATION_ERROR\",\n    \"message\": \"Title is required\",\n    \"details\": []\n  }\n}\n```\n\nSome endpoints still return the legacy v1-style shape:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"error\": \"not_found\",\n  \"message\": \"Task not found\"\n}\n```\n\nWrite a parser that accepts both: if `error` is an object, read `error.code` and `error.message`; if it is a string, read the sibling `message`. The legacy format is transitional and will be removed.\n\n## 10. Migration checklist\n\n1. Update base URL to `https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2` everywhere.\n2. Replace the `X-API-Key` header with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; if you adopt the login flow, implement refresh-on-401 and MFA handling.\n3. Rename fields: `desc`, `assigned_to`, `project`, `deadline`, `user_id`, `org` (§3).\n4. Convert Unix timestamps to ISO 8601 on send; parse ISO 8601 on receive, with explicit handling for project `created` and user `last_login` (§4).\n5. Switch pagination to `page`/`per_page` and unwrap the `data`/`meta` envelope on the tasks list.\n6. Expect `201 Created` (not `200 OK`) from task and project creation, and `204 No Content` from deletions.\n7. Change task assignment from `PUT .../assign` to `POST .../assign` with `assignee_id`.\n8. Move comment and history reads to `?include=`; plan for the missing comment-write endpoint (§8).\n9. Handle `409 Conflict` on task updates with a re-fetch-and-retry loop.\n10. Make `DELETE /projects/{id}` explicit about `cascade` for your safety posture.\n11. Update search calls to `GET /search/tasks` and remove the `type` parameter.\n12. Re-register webhooks with the expanded event list and add HMAC verification; subscribe only to declared events (§7).\n13. Parse both error formats (§9).\n14. Handle `429` with backoff using `X-RateLimit-Remaining`.\n\n## 11. Task events

task.createdDeclared + observed

Description
Fires when a new task is created in any project your webhook can access.
Trigger condition
A POST /tasks request succeeds (201 Created), or a task is created through the TaskFlow UI or a project template.

  "event": "task.created",
  "timestamp": "2024-03-01T14:22:00Z",

    "project_id": 12,
    "actor_id": 57
  }
}

task.updatedDeclared + observed

Description
Fires when one or more fields of an existing task change.
Trigger condition

Example payload

  "event": "task.updated",

    "actor_id": 57
  }

task.assignedDeclared + observed

Trigger condition

  "event": "task.assigned",
  "timestamp": "2024-03-05T10:02:00Z",
  "webhook_id": 301,
  "data": {
    "task_id": 1050,
    "assignee_id": 93,
    "actor_id": 57
  }
}
Reconstructed from delivery d-90006 (HTTP 200)

task.commentedDeclared + observed

Description
Fires when a comment is added to a task.
Trigger condition

Example payload
{
  "event": "task.commented",
  "timestamp": "2024-03-02T09:17:44Z",
  "webhook_id": 301,
  "data": {
    "task_id": 1042,
    "comment_id": 5567,
    "actor_id": 82
  }
}

task.deletedDeclared + observed

Fires when a task is permanently deleted. Delivered after the deletion, so the referenced task no longer exists.

}

Trigger condition
Daily scheduled check after midnight UTC once the due date has passed. Production evidence: fired at 00:00:00Z with days_overdue: 1.

  "event": "task.overdue",
  "timestamp": "2024-03-16T00:00:00Z",

  "data": {

    "due_date": "2024-03-15T00:00:00Z",

project.createdDeclared + observed

  }
}

member.addedDeclared + observed

    "actor_id": 57
  }

{
  "event": "member.removed",
  "timestamp": "2024-03-07T14:10:00Z",
  "webhook_id": 301,
  "data": {
    "project_id": 12,
    "user_id": 45,
    "actor_id": 57
  }
}

1: # TaskFlow API Documentation
2: 
3: **Version**: 2.0
4: **Last Updated**: March 2024
5: 
6: Welcome to the TaskFlow API! This document describes how to interact with our REST API for managing tasks and projects. You can use these endpoints to build integrations with TaskFlow.
7: 
8: ## Authentication
9: 
10: All API calls require a valid API key. Include your key in the `Authorization` header:
11: 
12: ```
13: Authorization: Bearer <your_api_key>
14: ```
15: 
16: You can generate an API key from the TaskFlow dashboard under Settings > API Keys.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## Tasks
21: 
22: ### GET /api/v2/tasks
23: 
24: Retrieves a list of tasks for the authenticated user. The user can filter results using query parameters.
25: 
26: **Query Parameters**
27: 
28: | Parameter | Type | Description |
29: |-----------|------|-------------|
30: | status | string | Filter by task status. Allowed values: `open`, `in_progress`, `done`, `archived` |
31: | project_id | integer | Only return tasks belonging to this project |
32: | page | integer | Page number for pagination (default: 1) |
33: | per_page | integer | Number of results per page (default: 20, max: 100) |
34: | sort | string | Sort field. One of `created_at`, `updated_at`, `priority` |
35: | order | string | Sort direction: `asc` or `desc` |
36: 
37: **Example Request**
38: 
39: ```bash
40: curl -X GET "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks?status=open&page=1" \
41:   -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"
42: ```
43: 
44: **Response** (200 OK)
45: 
46: ```json
47: {
48:   "data": [
49:     {
50:       "id": 1042,
51:       "title": "Fix login bug",
52:       "description": "Users are unable to login with SSO",
53:       "status": "open",
54:       "priority": "high",
55:       "assignee_id": 57,
56:       "project_id": 12,
57:       "created_at": "2024-03-01T14:22:00Z",
58:       "updated_at": "2024-03-01T14:22:00Z",
59:       "due_date": "2024-03-15T00:00:00Z"
60:     }
61:   ],
62:   "meta": {
63:     "current_page": 1,
64:     "total_pages": 5,
65:     "total_count": 98
66:   }
67: }
68: ```
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ### POST /api/v2/tasks
73: 
74: Creates a new task. You must provide at least a title. The task will be created under the user's default project if `project_id` is not specified.
75: 
76: **Request Body Arguments**
77: 
78: - `title` (string, **required**) - The title of the task. Max 255 characters.
79: - `description` (string) - A longer description. Supports Markdown formatting.
80: - `status` (string) - Initial status. Defaults to `open`.
81: - `priority` (string) - One of: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `critical`. Default is `medium`.
82: - `assignee_id` (integer) - User ID to assign the task to.
83: - `project_id` (integer) - Project to create the task in.
84: - `due_date` (string) - Due date in ISO 8601 format.
85: - `tags` (array of strings) - Tags to apply to the task.
86: 
87: **Example**
88: 
89: ```python
90: import requests
91: 
92: resp = requests.post(
93:     "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks",
94:     headers={"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"},
95:     json={
96:         "title": "Design new landing page",
97:         "description": "Create mockups for the Q2 marketing campaign",
98:         "priority": "high",
99:         "project_id": 12,
100:         "due_date": "2024-04-01T00:00:00Z",
101:         "tags": ["design", "marketing"]
102:     }
103: )
104: print(resp.json())
105: ```
106: 
107: Returns `201 Created` on success with the full task object in the response body.
108: 
109: **Errors**
110: 
111: | Status Code | Meaning |
112: |------------|---------|
113: | 400 | Bad request - missing required fields or invalid values |
114: | 401 | Authentication failed |
115: | 422 | Validation error (e.g. title too long) |
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ### GET /api/v2/tasks/{id}
120: 
121: Get a single task by its ID.
122: 
123: Pass the task ID as a path parameter. Returns the task object if found. Returns 404 if the task doesn't exist or you don't have access.
124: 
125: Response includes the full task object (same schema as list endpoint).
126: 
127: No additional arguments.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: ### Updating a task - PUT /api/v2/tasks/{id}
132: 
133: We support partial updates - you only need to send the fields you want to change. Any fields not included in the request body will remain unchanged.
134: 
135: Note: the `id` and `created_at` fields cannot be modified.
136: 
137: **Fields you can update:**
138: 
139: - title
140: - description
141: - status (must be a valid status string)
142: - priority
143: - assignee_id (set to `null` to unassign)
144: - project_id
145: - due_date (ISO 8601 timestamp or null to clear)
146: - tags
147: 
148: **Sample curl command:**
149: 
150: ```bash
151: curl -X PUT "https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/tasks/1042" \
152:   -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
153:   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
154:   -d '{"status": "in_progress", "assignee_id": 57}'
155: ```
156: 
157: The API returns `200 OK` and the updated task object on success.
158: 
159: ---
160: 
161: ### DELETE /api/v2/tasks/{id}
162: 
163: Permanently deletes a task. This action cannot be undone.
164: 
165: The user must have admin or owner permissions on the project that the task belongs to. Regular members can only delete tasks they created.
166: 
167: **Returns:**
168: 
169: `204 No Content` on success. The response body is empty.
170: 
171: If the task is not found a `404` error is returned. Attempting to delete a task without sufficient permissions results in `403 Forbidden`.
172: 
173: ---
174: 
175: ## Projects
176: 
177: ### List projects
178: 
179: ```
180: GET /api/v2/projects
181: ```
182: 
183: This route returns all projects the authenticated user has access to. Projects are returned in alphabetical order by name.
184: 
185: **Query args:**
186: 
187: - `archived` (boolean) - if `true`, include archived projects. Default `false`.
188: - `role` (string) - filter by the user's role in the project: `owner`, `admin`, `member`
189: 
190: No authentication header examples are given here since it follows the same pattern described at the top of this doc.
191: 
192: **Sample response:**
193: 
194: ```json
195: {
196:   "projects": [
197:     {
198:       "id": 12,
199:       "name": "Website Redesign",
200:       "description": "Q2 2024 website overhaul",
201:       "owner_id": 57,
202:       "created": 1709312400,
203:       "member_count": 8,
204:       "task_count": 45,
205:       "archived": false
206:     }
207:   ]
208: }
209: ```
210: 
211: Note that the `created` field here returns a Unix timestamp. We plan to migrate this to ISO 8601 in a future release.
212: 
213: ---
214: 
215: ### Create Project
216: 
217: **Endpoint:** `POST /api/v2/projects`
218: 
219: To create a new project, send a POST request with the following payload:
220: 
221: ```json
222: {
223:   "name": "My New Project",
224:   "description": "Optional project description"
225: }
226: ```
227: 
228: The `name` field is required and must be unique within the user's organization. Max 100 chars.
229: 
230: **Response fields:**
231: 
232: | Field | Type | Notes |
233: |-------|------|-------|
234: | id | integer | Auto-generated project ID |
235: | name | string | The project name |
236: | description | string | May be null |
237: | owner_id | integer | ID of creating user |
238: | created | integer | Unix timestamp |
239: | member_count | integer | Always 1 for new projects |
240: | task_count | integer | Always 0 for new projects |
241: | archived | boolean | Always false for new projects |
242: 
243: Returns HTTP 201.
244: 
245: No error documentation is provided here but the API follows standard REST conventions for error responses.
246: 
247: ---
248: 
249: ## User Info
250: 
251: ### Getting your profile
252: 
253: **Route**: GET /api/v2/users/me
254: 
255: This returns information about the currently authenticated user. Pass your API key as usual.
256: 
257: The response looks like:
258: 
259: ```json
260: {
261:   "user": {
262:     "id": 57,
263:     "email": "jane@example.com",
264:     "name": "Jane Smith",
265:     "role": "admin",
266:     "organization_id": 5,
267:     "timezone": "America/New_York",
268:     "created_at": "2023-01-15T09:00:00Z",
269:     "last_login": 1709398800
270:   }
271: }
272: ```
273: 
274: Note: `created_at` is ISO 8601 but `last_login` is a Unix timestamp. This inconsistency will be addressed in API v3.
275: 
276: ---
277: 
278: ## Rate Limiting
279: 
280: We enforce rate limits to ensure fair usage of the API. The current limits are:
281: 
282: - 100 requests per minute for free tier
283: - 1000 requests per minute for paid plans
284: 
285: When you exceed the limit, the API returns `429 Too Many Requests`. Check the `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header to see how many requests you have left.
286: 
287: ## Pagination
288: 
289: List endpoints support pagination via `page` and `per_page` query parameters. The response `meta` object contains pagination info. Note that the projects endpoint does not currently support pagination - all projects are returned in a single response.
290: 
291: ## Errors
292: 
293: The API uses standard HTTP status codes. Error responses include a JSON body:
294: 
295: ```json
296: {
297:   "error": {
298:     "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
299:     "message": "Title is required",
300:     "details": []
301:   }
302: }
303: ```
304: 
305: However, some older endpoints may return errors in a different format:
306: 
307: ```json
308: {
309:   "error": "not_found",
310:   "message": "Task not found"
311: }
312: ```
313: 
314: We are working on standardizing error responses across all routes.
315: 
316: ---
317: 
318: *For questions or support, email api-support@taskflow.io*

1: # TaskFlow API v1
2: 
3: API base URL: `https://api.taskflow.io/api`
4: 
5: Auth: use `X-API-Key` header with your key.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## GET /api/tasks
10: 
11: Gets tasks. Returns JSON array.
12: 
13: Params: `status`, `project`, `limit`, `offset`
14: 
15: Response: array of task objects.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## POST /api/tasks
20: 
21: Create a task.
22: 
23: Body: JSON with `title` (required), `desc`, `status`, `priority`, `assigned_to`, `project`, `deadline`.
24: 
25: `deadline` should be a Unix timestamp.
26: 
27: Returns the created task. 200 OK.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## GET /api/tasks/:id
32: 
33: Fetch one task.
34: 
35: ---
36: 
37: ## PUT /api/tasks/:id
38: 
39: Update task fields. Send only what changed.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## DELETE /api/tasks/:id
44: 
45: Delete a task. Must be owner.
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## GET /api/projects
50: 
51: List all projects.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## POST /api/projects
56: 
57: Make a new project. Body: `name` (required), `desc`.
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## GET /api/users/current
62: 
63: Get current user info.
64: 
65: Response:
66: 
67: ```
68: {
69:   "id": 57,
70:   "email": "jane@example.com",
71:   "name": "Jane Smith",
72:   "role": "admin",
73:   "org": 5
74: }
75: ```
76: 
77: ---
78: 
79: ## GET /api/tasks/:id/comments
80: 
81: List comments on a task.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## POST /api/tasks/:id/comments
86: 
87: Add comment. Body: `text`.
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ## GET /api/search
92: 
93: Search across tasks and projects.
94: 
95: Params: `q` (search query), `type` (task or project)
96: 
97: ---
98: 
99: ## PUT /api/tasks/:id/assign
100: 
101: Assign a task to a user. Body: `user_id`.
102: 
103: This is a convenience endpoint. You can also update the `assigned_to` field directly via PUT /api/tasks/:id.
104: 
105: ---
106: 
107: ## GET /api/tasks/:id/history
108: 
109: Returns change history for a task. Each entry shows what field changed, old value, new value, who changed it, and when (Unix timestamp).
110: 
111: ---
112: 
113: ## DELETE /api/projects/:id
114: 
115: Delete a project. All tasks in the project will also be deleted.
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ## Errors
120: 
121: Errors return JSON: `{"error": "message"}`.
122: 
123: Common codes: 400, 401, 404, 500.
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## Webhooks
128: 
129: POST /api/webhooks - register a webhook. Body: `url`, `events` (array).
130: 
131: GET /api/webhooks - list webhooks.
132: 
133: DELETE /api/webhooks/:id - remove a webhook.
134: 
135: Events: `task.created`, `task.updated`, `task.deleted`, `project.created`.
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## Notes
140: 
141: - Rate limit: 60 req/min.
142: - All timestamps are Unix.
143: - Contact support@taskflow.io for help.

(End of file - total 143 lines)
</content>", "type": "text"}]

1: # RESTAPIDocs Examples
2: 
3: These examples were taken from projects mainly using [Django Rest
4: Framework](https://github.com/tomchristie/django-rest-framework) and so the
5: JSON responses are often similar to the way in which DRF makes responses.
6: 
7: Where full URLs are provided in responses they will be rendered as if service
8: is running on 'http://testserver/'.
9: 
10: ## Open Endpoints
11: 
12: Open endpoints require no Authentication.
13: 
14: * [Login](login.md) : `POST /api/login/`
15: 
16: ## Endpoints that require Authentication
17: 
18: Closed endpoints require a valid Token to be included in the header of the
19: request. A Token can be acquired from the Login view above.
20: 
21: ### Current User related
22: 
23: Each endpoint manipulates or displays information related to the User whose
24: Token is provided with the request:
25: 
26: * [Show info](user/get.md) : `GET /api/user/`
27: * [Update info](user/put.md) : `PUT /api/user/`
28: 
29: ### Account related
30: 
31: Endpoints for viewing and manipulating the Accounts that the Authenticated User
32: has permissions to access.
33: 
34: * [Show Accessible Accounts](accounts/get.md) : `GET /api/accounts/`
35: * [Create Account](accounts/post.md) : `POST /api/accounts/`
36: * [Show An Account](accounts/pk/get.md) : `GET /api/accounts/:pk/`
37: * [Update An Account](accounts/pk/put.md) : `PUT /api/accounts/:pk/`
38: * [Delete An Account](accounts/pk/delete.md) : `DELETE /api/accounts/:pk/`
39: # Show Current User
40: 
41: Get the details of the currently Authenticated User along with basic
42: subscription information.
43: 
44: **URL** : `/api/user/`
45: 
46: **Method** : `GET`
47: 
48: **Auth required** : YES
49: 
50: **Permissions required** : None
51: 
52: ## Success Response
53: 
54: **Code** : `200 OK`
55: 
56: **Content examples**
57: 
58: For a User with ID 1234 on the local database where that User has saved an
59: email address and name information.
60: 
61: ```json
62: {
63:     "id": 1234,
64:     "first_name": "Joe",
65:     "last_name": "Bloggs",
66:     "email": "joe25@example.com"
67: }
68: ```
69: 
70: For a user with ID 4321 on the local database but no details have been set yet.
71: 
72: ```json
73: {
74:     "id": 4321,
75:     "first_name": "",
76:     "last_name": "",
77:     "email": ""
78: }
79: ```
80: 
81: ## Notes
82: 
83: * If the User does not have a `UserInfo` instance when requested then one will
84:   be created for them.
85: 404: Not Found404: Not Found404: Not Found404: Not Found

1: ---
2: stage: none
3: group: unassigned
4: info: For assistance with this Style Guide page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments-to-other-projects-and-subjects>.
5: description: Writing styles, markup, formatting, and other standards for the GitLab RESTful APIs.
6: title: Documenting REST API resources
7: ---
8: 
9: REST API resources are documented in Markdown under
10: [`/doc/api`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api). Each
11: resource has its own Markdown file, which is linked from
12: [`api_resources.md`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/doc/api/api_resources.md).
13: 
14: When modifying the Markdown or API code, also update the corresponding
15: [OpenAPI definition](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/tree/master/doc/api/openapi), by running
16: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:generate` and `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:generate`.
17: To check if the OpenAPI definition needs to be updated, you can run `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v2:check_docs` and
18: `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:check_docs`.
19: This is also checked by the `openapi-doc-check` CI/CD job that runs for commits that modify API code or documentation.
20: 
21: The Markdown topic for an API resource must include:
22: 
23: - A block that includes the HTTP method (like GET, PUT, DELETE) followed by the request path. Always start the path with a `/`. For example:
24: 
25:   ```plaintext
26:   GET /api/v4/projects/:id/repository/branches
27:   ```
28: 
29: - A detailed [description of the attributes](#request-attributes).
30: - A detailed [description of the response body](#response-attributes).
31: - A cURL example.
32: - A response body example (in JSON format).
33: 
34: After a new API documentation page is added, [add an entry in the global navigation](site_architecture/global_nav.md#add-a-navigation-entry).
35: 
36: ## Page metadata
37: 
38: When you create a new page, include a `description` metadata field
39: in the front matter that follows these guidelines for consistency:
40: 
41: - Start with "REST API to"
42: - Use action verbs that describe what users can do with the API
43: - Avoid words ending in -ing
44: - Keep to one sentence, ideally under 100 characters
45: - End with a period
46: 
47: For example:
48: 
49: ```yaml
50: ---
51: stage: Example Stage
52: group: Example Group
53: info: To determine the technical writer assigned to the Stage/Group associated with this page, see <https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product/ux/technical-writing/#assignments>
54: description: REST API to create, update, and delete issues.
55: title: Example page title
56: ---
57: ```
58: 
59: Additional examples:
60: 
61: - `description: REST API to retrieve CI/CD job details, retry and cancel jobs, run manual jobs, and access job logs.`
62: - `description: REST API to create, manage, and monitor CI/CD pipelines.`
63: 
64: ## API topic template
65: 
66: Use the following template to help you get started. Be sure to list any
67: required attributes first in the table.
68: 
69: ````markdown
70: ## API name
71: 
72: {{</* history */>}}
73:

305: ## cURL commands
306: 
307: - Use `https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/` as an endpoint.
308: - Wherever needed use this personal access token: `<your_access_token>`.
309: - Always put the request first. `GET` is the default so you don't have to

312:   [`scripts/lint-doc.sh`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/scripts/lint-doc.sh).)
313: - Declare URLs with the `--url` parameter, and wrap the URL in double quotes (`"`).
314: - Prefer to use examples using the personal access token and don't pass data of
315:   username and password.
316: - For legibility, use the ` \ ` character and indentation to break long single-line
317:   commands apart into multiple lines.
318: 
319: | Methods                                         | Description                                            |
320: |-------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
321: | `--header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>"` | Use this method as is, whenever authentication needed. |
322: | `--request POST`                                | Use this method when creating new objects.             |

326: ## cURL Examples
327: 
328: The following sections include a set of [cURL](https://curl.se/) examples
329: you can use in the API documentation.
330: 
331: > [!warning]
332: > Do not use information for real users, URLs, or tokens. For documentation, refer to our
333: > relevant style guide sections on [fake user information](styleguide/_index.md#fake-user-information),
334: > [fake URLs](styleguide/_index.md#fake-urls), and [fake tokens](styleguide/_index.md#fake-tokens).
335: 
336: ### Simple cURL command
337: 
338: Get the details of a group:
339: 
340: ```shell
341: curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
342:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups/gitlab-org"
343: ```
344: 
345: ### cURL example with parameters passed in the URL
346: 
347: Create a new project under the authenticated user's namespace:
348: 
349: ```shell
350: curl --request POST --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
351:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects?name=foo"
352: ```
353: 
354: ### Post data using cURL's `--data`
355: 
356: Instead of using `--request POST` and appending the parameters to the URI, you
357: can use cURL's `--data` option. The example below creates a new project
358: `foo` under the authenticated user's namespace.
359: 
360: ```shell
361: curl --data "name=foo" \
362:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
363:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects"
364: ```
365: 
366: ### Post data using cURL's `--data-urlencode`
367: 
368: Use `--data-urlencode` when the data contains special characters that require URL encoding.
369: 
370: You can use this option for:
371: 
372: - Markdown content with code blocks or special formatting.
373: - Regular expressions containing `+`, `.`, or `*`.
374: - Text with quotes, ampersands, or other reserved URL characters.
375: - File content that might contain special characters.
376: 
377: For alphanumeric data without special characters, use [`--data`](#post-data-using-curls---data) instead.
378: 
379: For an attribute with special characters:
380: 
381: ```shell
382: curl --request POST \
383:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
384:   --data-urlencode "description=Fix issue with 'quotes' & ampersands" \
385:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/issues"
386: ```
387: 
388: For content with regular expression patterns:
389: 
390: ```shell
391: curl --request DELETE \
392:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
393:   --data-urlencode "name_regex_delete=dev-.+" \
394:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/5/registry/repositories/2/tags"
395: ```
396: 
397: For content from a file, use `attribute@filename`:
398: 
399: ```shell
400: curl --request POST \
401:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
402:   --data-urlencode "title=API documentation update" \
403:   --data-urlencode "content@content.md" \
404:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/1/wikis"
405: ```
406: 
407: ### Post data using JSON content
408: 
409: This example creates a new group. Be aware of the use of single (`'`) and double
410: (`"`) quotes.
411: 
412: ```shell
413: curl --request POST \
414:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
415:   --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
416:   --data '{"path": "my-group", "name": "My group"}' \
417:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups"
418: ```
419: 
420: For readability, you can also set up the `--data` by using the following format:
421: 
422: ```shell
423: curl --request POST \
424:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/groups" \
425:   --header "content-type: application/json" \
426:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
427:   --data '{
428:     "path": "my-group",
429:     "name": "My group"
430: }'
431: ```
432: 
433: ### Post data using form-data
434: 
435: Instead of using JSON or URL-encoding data, you can use `multipart/form-data` which
436: properly handles data encoding:
437: 
438: ```shell
439: curl --request POST \
440:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
441:   --form "title=ssh-key" \
442:   --form "key=ssh-rsa AAAAB3NzaC1yc2EA..." \
443:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/users/25/keys"
444: ```
445: 
446: The above example adds an SSH public key titled `ssh-key` to the account of
447: a user with ID 25. The operation requires administrator access.
448: 
449: ### Escape special characters
450: 
451: Spaces or slashes (`/`) can sometimes result in errors, so you should
452: escape them when possible. In the example below we create a new issue which
453: contains spaces in its title. Observe how spaces are escaped using the `%20`
454: ASCII code.
455: 
456: ```shell
457: curl --request POST \
458:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>" \
459:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/42/issues?title=Hello%20GitLab"
460: ```
461: 
462: Use `%2F` for slashes (`/`).
463: 
464: ### Pass arrays to API calls
465: 
466: The GitLab API sometimes accepts arrays of strings or integers. For example, to
467: exclude specific users when requesting a list of users for a project, you would
468: do something like this:
469: 
470: ```shell
471: curl --request PUT \
472:   --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <your_access_token>"
473:   --data "skip_users[]=<user_id>" \
474:   --data "skip_users[]=<user_id>" \
475:   --url "https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/<project_id>/users"
476: ```

Governs every endpoint page produced by the Technical Writing team.\\n**Sources of grounding:** The in-house `restapidocs_combined_template.md` endpoint template, the [GitLab REST API documentation guidelines](../task_folder/references/gitlab_api_doc_styleguide.md) snapshot, and the findings recorded in `doc_audit_tracker.csv`.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1. Purpose and scope\\n\\nThis guide exists because TaskFlow's API documentation was historically written ad-hoc by individual developers. The 2025 documentation audit (`doc_audit_tracker.csv`) found that of 17 audited endpoint rows, 6 required full rewrites, 7 required updates, and only 4 were acceptable as-is. The most common failure modes were not factual errors but *inconsistency*: two reviewers described the same object with different words (\\\"user\\\" vs. \\\"assignee\\\"), three different formatting styles were used for the same kind of information (tables, bullets, prose), and six pages drifted between active and passive voice.\\n\\nThis guide eliminates those failures by fixing a single canonical pattern for every endpoint page. If a rule here conflicts with an individual author's preference, this guide wins. If a rule here conflicts with verified product behavior, product behavior wins and this guide must be amended.\\n\\n## 2. Source-of-truth hierarchy\\n\\nTaskFlow documents one API from several sources. When sources disagree, resolve them in this order:\\n\\n1. **The OpenAPI specification** (`taskflow_openapi_v2_extract.yaml`) is the machine-readable contract extracted from the codebase. Parameter names, types, enums, defaults, requiredness, and declared status codes come from the spec.\\n2. **Verified production behavior** (delivery logs, trace captures) is authoritative for behavior the spec does not model, such as webhook retry policy. Never publish production-derived behavior without labeling its provenance.\\n3. **Prose documentation** is the presentation layer. It may add context, examples, and warnings, but it must never contradict the spec. Any docs-only claim (for example, \\\"tasks are created in the user's default project when `project_id` is omitted\\\") that is not backed by the spec must be tagged for engineering verification before publication.\\n4. **The audit tracker** is a quality-control instrument, not a source of truth. Its notes reveal gaps that a plain diff of spec versus docs cannot (terminology drift, missing examples, inconsistent formatting). Every row must reach `acceptable` status before the docs it describes may ship.\\n\\nRule of engagement: **docs may say more than the spec, never less and never differently.** If the spec knows something the docs do not, that is a documentation bug. If the docs know something the spec does not, file a spec-backfill ticket (see \u00a715).\\n\\n## 3. Page structure\\n\\nEvery endpoint page follows the combined template's skeleton, hardened with GitLab-style attribute tables. The mandatory order is:\\n\\n1. **H2 resource section** (for example, `## Tasks`) opening with the sentence pattern `Use this API to <verb> <feature>\u2026`, per the GitLab introduction convention. Example: *\\\"Use this API to create, read, update, and delete tasks, the primary work units in TaskFlow.\\\"*\\n2. **H3 operation section** per HTTP method. Each operation contains, in order:\\n   - Operation title (see \u00a74).\\n   - A method-and-path block in a fenced `plaintext` code block, path always beginning with `/`:\\n     ```plaintext\\n     POST /api/v2/tasks\\n     ```\\n   - One-sentence description whose first sentence broadly restates the title (GitLab convention: \\\"List all tasks\\\" \u2192 \\\"Lists all tasks.\\\").\\n   - Request attributes table (path parameters first, then query/body; required attributes first, then alphabetical). See \u00a75.\\n   - Success statement and response attributes, if the response body carries meaningful fields.\\n   - Example request (cURL).\\n   - Example response (JSON).\\n   - Error table.\\n3. **Cross-cutting H2 sections** collected once, not repeated per endpoint: Authentication, Rate limiting, Pagination, Errors, Timestamps and formats, Webhook delivery guarantees.\\n\\nThe page index must list every operation in the form used by the combined template \u2014 `* [Operation title](anchor) : `METHOD /path`` \u2014 grouped into *Open endpoints* (no auth) and *Endpoints that require authentication*, so readers can orient before diving in.\\n\\n## 4. Operation titles\\n\\nStart every operation title with the canonical verb for its HTTP method (adapted from GitLab):\\n\\n| HTTP method | Verb | Alternatives (use sparingly) | Example |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| `GET` (multiple) | List | | **List tasks** |\\n| `GET` (single) | Retrieve | Get | **Retrieve a task** |\\n| `POST` | Create | Add | **Create a task** |\\n| `PUT` | Update | Replace | **Update a task** |\\n| `DELETE` | Delete | | **Delete a task** |\\n\\nForbidden constructions: headings phrased as sentences (\\\"Updating a task \u2014 PUT \u2026\\\"), gerunds (\\\"Getting your profile\\\"), and synonyms that drift by page. The audit tracker flagged exactly this drift: *modify* in one body, *update* in a title; *remove* in a description, *delete* everywhere else. One verb per method, always.\\n\\n## 5. Attribute tables\\n\\nAll request and response parameters are documented in Markdown tables, never in bullet lists. The audit tracker shows bullet-list parameters correlate with the lowest completeness scores (40\u201355%).\\n\\n**Request columns:** `Attribute | Type | Required | Description`.\\n**Response columns:** `Attribute | Type | Description`.\\n\\nRules:\\n\\n- Attribute names in backticks. Types use the OpenAPI vocabulary: `string`, `integer`, `boolean`, `string array`, `integer array`, `object`.\\n- Path attributes first, then required attributes, then the rest alphabetically.\\n- `Required` takes `Yes`, `No`, or `Conditional`. For conditional attributes, define the attribute first, then state the dependency in the canonical form: *\\\"Required if `mfa_enabled` is `true`.\\\"*\\n- Every attribute gets a meaningful description. Vague stubs (\\\"The ID\\\", \\\"The name\\\") are audit failures. State defaults as *\\\"Default is `25`.\\\"* State enums exhaustively with backticked values, even when a companion table exists.\\n- Nullable attributes: state what `null` means \u2014 *\\\"Set to `null` to unassign the task.\\\"*\\n- Nested objects use dot notation in response tables: `meta.current_page`, `data[].assignee_id`.\\n\\n## 6. Examples\\n\\nEvery operation carries **at least one cURL example and one JSON response example.** The audit tracker's six `needs_rewrite` rows all lacked one or both.\\n\\ncURL conventions (GitLab-derived, adapted to TaskFlow):\\n\\n- Base URL is always `https://api.taskflow.io/api/v2/`.\\n- Credentials are always the placeholder `<your_api_token>`; never real-looking tokens, emails, or URLs.\\n- Use long option names: `--header`, `--request`, `--data`, `--url`. Never `-H`, `-X`, `-d` in reference docs.\\n- Always put the URL in `--url \\\"\u2026\\\"`. For `GET`, omit `--request` (GET is the default); include `--request` for POST/PUT/DELETE.\\n- Break long commands with ` \\\\` and two-space indentation.\\n- Send JSON with an explicit `--header \\\"Content-Type: application/json\\\"` and single-quoted `--data '{\\\"\u2026\\\"}'`.\\n- URL-encode spaces and reserved characters (`%20`, `%2F`).\\n\\nResponse examples must be realistic, minimal, and consistent with each other: the task with ID `1042`, project `12`, user `57` recur across TaskFlow examples so readers can follow one fixture through the whole document. Show at most two objects in list responses.\\n\\nLanguage-specific SDK examples (Python, JavaScript) are welcome as *additions* but never as replacements for cURL + JSON.\\n\\n## 7. Status codes and errors\\n\\n- Begin the success statement with the GitLab formula: *\\\"If successful, returns `200 OK` and the following response attributes:\\\"* (adjust the code: `201 Created`, `204 No Content`).\\n- Every operation ends with an error table: `Status code | Meaning | Common causes`. \\\"The API follows standard REST conventions\\\" is not documentation; enumerate the codes the spec declares, plus `401` and `429` where relevant.\\n- `409 Conflict` must be documented wherever concurrent modification can occur, with recovery guidance (re-`GET`, re-apply, retry).\\n- Error bodies: the canonical v2 envelope is\\n  ```json\\n  { \\\"error\\\": { \\\"code\\\": \\\"VALIDATION_ERROR\\\", \\\"message\\\": \\\"Title is required\\\", \\\"details\\\": [] } }\\n  ```\\n  Document the legacy flat format (`{\\\"error\\\": \\\"not_found\\\", \\\"message\\\": \\\"\u2026\\\"}`) only where it still occurs, and always label it as transitional.\\n\\n## 8. Voice, tense, and grammar\\n\\n- Present tense, indicative mood, active voice. The audit tracker's `voice_consistency` column flagged six rows; the fix is mechanical: *\\\"Retrieves a task\\\"* not *\\\"This endpoint can be used to retrieve a task\\\"* or *\\\"You can fetch a task.\\\"*\\n- Address the reader as *you*. Never *we* for the API's actions (\\\"we delete the tasks\\\") \u2014 the API *deletes*.\\n- Sentence case for all headings. American spelling. Serial (Oxford) comma.\\n- Second person for instructions; third person for system behavior.\\n- Do not personify the API. It *returns*, *rejects*, *requires* \u2014 it does not *want* or *allow politely*.\\n\\n## 9. Terminology glossary (canonical terms)\\n\\nThe audit tracker recorded twelve terminology conflicts. These are now settled:\\n\\n| \u2705 Canonical | \u274c Banned variants | Rationale |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| retrieve | fetch, get (in prose) | Matches operation titles |\\n| endpoint | route, URL (as a noun for an operation) | One noun per concept |\\n| task ID | taskId, task_id (in prose) | `taskId` only as a literal path parameter name, in backticks |\\n| update | modify, change (as the operation verb) | Verb table in \u00a74 |\\n| assignee | user (when discussing assignment) | Distinguishes from actors/watchers |\\n| delete | remove | Verb table in \u00a74 |\\n| webhook URL | callback URL, destination | One name for the subscriber's endpoint |\\n| access token | JWT (in prose) | Implementation detail, not a contract term |\\n| token refresh | token rotation | Rotation implies a different algorithm |\\n| filter (list endpoints) | query (for list parameters) | Reserve *query* for the search endpoint |\\n| request body | payload, body (interchangeably) | Pick one; use *payload* only for webhooks |\\n| watcher | follower, observer | Matches `watchers` field name |\\n\\nWhen a spec field name exists (`assignee_id`, `due_date`), the prose must use it verbatim, in backticks.\\n\\n## 10. Timestamps and data formats\\n\\n- The TaskFlow v2 standard is **ISO 8601 UTC**, rendered with a trailing `Z`: `2024-03-01T14:22:00Z`.\\n- Known legacy deviations are documented where they occur, with a warning, not silently: project `created` and user `last_login` are Unix timestamps pending normalization (tracked for v3). Never describe a deviation as \\\"fine\\\" \u2014 describe it, flag it, and give the conversion hint.\\n- IDs are integers. Enums are lowercase snake_case (`in_progress`, `task.created`). Dates in *filters* use `YYYY-MM-DD`.\\n\\n## 11. Webhooks documentation\\n\\nWebhook events are documented in the published **Webhook Event Catalog** (HTML), which is the single authoritative list. Rules:\\n\\n- Event names use dot notation `resource.verb` (`task.created`, `member.added`). Never invent synonyms in prose.\\n- Every event entry documents: name, description, trigger condition, example payload, and provenance (declared in the OpenAPI spec, observed in the delivery log, or both). Provenance labels are mandatory because the catalog synthesizes contract and production reality; events observed in production but absent from the spec must be marked so integrators do not assume they are subscribable.\\n- Document retry behavior with its evidence source. As of the March 2024 export: failed deliveries are retried up to 3 times, then marked `failed`.\\n- Document HMAC payload verification whenever `secret` exists on the resource.\\n\\n## 12. Versioning, history, and deprecation\\n\\n- Every page carries a version line (`**API version:** 2.0.1`) and a last-reviewed date, mirroring the audit tracker's `last_reviewed` column so the two artifacts stay in lockstep.\\n- Additions and behavior changes get a short **History** note at the top of the affected section, in the GitLab pattern: *- `watchers` introduced in TaskFlow API 2.0.*\\n- Deprecations are announced in three places: inline in the attribute table (*\\\"[Deprecated](link) in 2.1. Use `due_date` instead.\\\"*), in the History note, and on the global deprecations list. Never delete a documented attribute without a replacement pointer.\\n\\n## 13. Rate limiting and pagination\\n\\n- Cross-cutting sections state the contract once: tier limits (100 requests/minute free, 1000/minute paid), the `429 Too Many Requests` response, and the `X-RateLimit-Remaining` response header.\\n- Pagination parameters are `page` (default `1`) and `per_page` (default `25`, maximum `200`). List responses carry a `meta` object (`current_page`, `total_pages`, `total_count`). Any list endpoint that deviates must say so explicitly \u2014 the current project list is the known case to watch.\\n\\n## 14. Accessibility and rendering\\n\\n- One idea per paragraph; tables over prose for enumerations; fenced code blocks always declare a language (`bash`, `json`, `plaintext`).\\n- Warn before destructive operations with a blockquote warning: `> [!warning]` followed by the consequence and any escape hatch (`cascade=false`).\\n- Links resolve within the docs set; anchors are GitHub-compatible (lowercase, hyphenated).\\n\\n## 15. Docs-only claims awaiting verification (see \u00a72.3) live in the report with status `Flagged for engineering`.\\n\\n## 16. Pre-publication checklist\\n\\nA page may ship only when every item holds \u2014 these mirror the audit tracker's columns so the tracker can be retired into a boolean gate:\\n\\n1. Description present and first sentence restates the title.\\n2. Auth requirement stated.\\n3. All path/query/body attributes in tables; spec-identical names, types, enums, defaults, requiredness.\\n4. cURL example and JSON response example present.\\n5. Error table complete against the spec, plus 401/429 where applicable.\\n6. Voice, terminology, and formatting conform to \u00a7\u00a74\u201310.\\n7. Any docs-only claim is tagged verified or flagged.\\n8.
